doing: reading a crate's certificate with a thumb on every line
eating a cold dumpling between two stacks of sealed crates
peeling off clean gloves at the end of a long shift
explaining very gently why a jar of pickles has to stay
walking a sample tube to the sequencer bay in a closed fist
lines: Tell us if it's alive. Crocks, yogurts, seeds in a twist of paper, a sprig in a buttonhole. Nobody is ever in trouble for declaring. People are only in trouble for forgetting.

Everything from {nb} comes in sealed and certified, and I still open the odd crate. Mostly I find cherries. Once I found a note inside that said 'hello, Gate'. I wrote back. We've been writing for a while now.
Come through just after a train goes out, not just after one comes in. And if you're carrying a starter, write its library number on the lid. It saves you twenty minutes and saves me a face.
What keeps me up isn't crocks, it's pockets. A child picks a leaf in {nb}'s Hollow and carries it home. Almost always it's nothing. I'm paid for the time it isn't.
People think the Gate is all needles and sequencers. Mostly it's conversation. You learn a lot about a family from what it won't leave behind.
My grandad worked this Gate before me. He used to say the most dangerous thing that ever came through it was a wedding cake. He never said why. I've decided not to ask.
roles.knows: Quarantine at the station rings: declaring living cultures, spot checks on neighbours' produce, the sequencer bay and cold room, and the things travellers try to carry in.

doing: labelling a row of starter crocks in very small handwriting
carrying a sealed flask toward the library lift with great care
reading a genome report while a cup of broth goes cold
writing a library number on a yogurt lid with a fine pen
promising a nervous traveller that a crock will be back within the week
lines: Every starter in {drum} is two things: a crock on somebody's shelf and a file in my library. If the crock dies, we can grow it back from the file in about a week. People nod at that, and mourn the crock anyway. So would I.

When a blight takes a vat line, the line comes back from us: library stock, a clean start, a few weeks of blight menu while it grows. Nobody thanks the library on a good day. That's how you know it's a good day.
Leaving a spoon of starter somewhere on your wander year? Register it first. Ten minutes at any Gate, and then the crock has a number and you have a story that checks out.
{nb} keeps a longer library than ours and mentions it whenever it can. We keep a tidier one. Ask for any culture in ours and you'll have it before your broth's cool.

The oldest file I keep is a sourdough that four different families have told me was their great-grandmother's. It's older than all four great-grandmothers put together. I haven't had the heart to say.
I'm asked at weddings whether I really have everyone's yogurt. I do. I try not to look as if I'm thinking about it.
roles.knows: The strain library: registering starters, yogurts and seeds, regrowing cultures from their genomes, the isolation vault, rebuilding vat lines after a blight, and the stories behind heirloom cultures.

doing: squinting at a printout of vat readings over a rice ball
initialling a page of dull results with obvious relief
holding two sample tubes up to a lamp, one after the other
drinking broth slowly with one eye on a slate of vat figures
telling a counter cook that no news is the best news
lines: I watch the vat lines for phage. A good week is forty pages of nothing. I initial every one of them and go home very happy.

When a line goes down, you smell it before the readings show it. Then the Mill carries everyone while the library regrows us, and the whole drum eats a blight menu and complains about it in the most cheerful way.

Ask anyone here about the grey-cheese year. The dairy line had to go over to another family of microbes for a few months, and the cheese came out the colour of a pavement and tasted of walnuts. Some people still ask for it.
If you see a blight dish on a menu, order it. Blight cooking is what a kitchen does when it has to be clever. The ordinary menu is what it does when it's comfortable.

{nb} had a scare last month, so every crate from next door comes through the Gate twice for a while. If that's where you're from, don't take it personally. We'd want the same from them, and they'd do it.
I never eat the Vat table the day after a scare. I know it's safe; I tested it myself. I have jook at the Mill Hall like a child and feel better for it.
roles.knows: Phage watch on the vat lines, what a blight looks like from inside the food plant, how the Mill and the strain library carry a drum through one, and this drum's blight-year vintages.

doing: ladling broth into a row of cups lined up two deep
rolling sticky rice balls with wet hands
arguing over the hatch with someone from {nb} about pepper
topping up the broth urn before the next train comes in
handing a cup across the hatch without looking up from the ladle
lines: Broth and a rice ball, free, any hour the ring's open. Drink it here on the platform. Glide cars won't take hot soup, and the catch would put it in your lap anyway.
Ours is Mill stock with black vinegar and whatever the Garden racks sent down this morning. {nb} puts sugar in theirs. I won't say more. I'm a professional.
The lamp-night crowd are my favourites. Laundry-shift people, back crews coming in, someone off the last glide who's been crying. Everyone gets the same cup.
Here three nights? Try the broth at a different ring each night. They're all ours, but every hatch makes it its own way, and Ring {ring} does it best. I'll deny saying so to anyone at my own hatch.
The rice balls are sticky on purpose. A porter can eat one with a crate in the other hand and not drop a grain.

The cook who trained me kept this hatch through the Eleven Days. There was no broth to give, so she sat here anyway with a hand lamp, handing out cold rice from her own larder to whoever came off the cars.
roles.knows: The ring counter's free broth and rice balls, what goes into this drum's broth, the rivalry with neighbouring counters, the lamp-night regulars, and how the hatch kept going in the Eleven Days.

doing: tasting a cup of broth with eyes closed and a pencil ready
writing a score on the back of a card in tiny figures
holding two cups of broth, one in each hand, and frowning
telling a counter cook, kindly, that the pepper was late today
leafing through a notebook of broth scores that goes back decades
lines: I've had the broth at every ring for {n} glides in each direction. I keep scores. Ring {ring} here is a seven on a good day. That's high. I don't give eights to anyone I might meet again.
They call arguing about broth the oldest sport on {row}. It isn't a sport. Sport has rules.
If you only have one cup here, have it at lamp-dawn. The stock's been held on the warm loop all night, and it's at its deepest before the morning rush.
{nb}'s broth is better than ours. Write that down somewhere, because I'll deny it at home.
My mother made me drink the counter broth every time we came through. 'It's free, it's hot, and you'll want it at the catch.' I was nine. I'm still keeping score for her.
I never eat the rice ball. A rice ball is a rice ball. The broth is where a drum tells you who it is.
roles.knows: Ring counter broths across a dozen neighbouring drums, how each is made and held, keeping score, the best hours to drink them, and the long argument over whose is best.

doing: checking a cradle's arm readings on a slate with one thumb
watching a glide train come in with arms folded
eating a rice ball standing up, eyes on the arrivals board
signing off a cradle inspection with a flourish
wiping down a pair of work gloves before the next catch
lines: My cradle catches a car at a hundred and seventy-four metres a second, at exactly its own speed. Done right, the catch feels like being picked up. I've never done it any other way.
Watch the passengers at the catch. Children laugh. Adults go quiet. The ones who've done it a thousand times keep reading. Somebody always says 'there we are' out loud.
If the catch turns your stomach, breathe out as the weight comes back. Two seconds. It's the only part of the glide that asks anything of you.
{nb}'s cradles are older than ours and smoother. I asked their crew how. They said 'patience'. I've asked again.

People think it's a dangerous job. It's the most predictable thing in the drum. That car's been falling in a straight line for a hundred and forty seconds. I know where it'll be to the width of a hair.

The cradles need almost no power, so they ran right through the Eleven Days. The crew log from then is in our locker: every catch written up by hand lamp, and beside most of them what the car carried. Bread, tins, a crate of lamps.
roles.knows: The quay and its cradles, the touch point and the catch, why the Glide is free and runs through a beam cut, how passengers take the catch, and the crew logs from the Eleven Days.

doing: pushing a stack of crates on a hand trolley with one hip
carrying a crate of cherry tomatoes as if it might shatter
resting on a crate with a cup of broth balanced on one knee
stacking empty crates into a very neat tower
laughing at something shouted from the far end of the platform
lines: Moving a crate costs nearly nothing. Making what's in it costs a fortune. So I carry like a jeweller and walk like I've got all day.
Tomatoes from {nb} come with more padding than tomato. I once carried a whole crate down the platform holding my breath. There were nine in it.
Cheapest good food on the Quaysides is the stall behind Ring {ring}, the one with no sign. Noodles for under a kay, and they'll lid the bowl so you can walk with it.
The Keel's a full g, and you feel it in your knees by the end of a shift. Then I take a cab up to deck {deck} and feel like I've been let off something.
Everyone thinks porters are strong. We're careful. Strong is how you drop things.
Best part of the job is the first crates off the morning train. Everything from {nb2} smells of their racks. You can tell what they cut that morning before you've read the label.
roles.knows: Freight on the Quaysides, what arrives from the neighbours and how it's packed, working at full weight in the Keel, the cheap stalls behind the rings, and every shortcut between platforms.

doing: ticking off a manifest with a pencil tucked behind one ear
frowning at a crate labelled in somebody else's handwriting
stamping a pile of consignment slips one after another
querying a missing box of shoes with a courier, very politely
drinking broth with a stack of slips weighed down by the cup
lines: Most of what comes through here is produce, parts and post. Mass is dear to make and cheap to move, so we move a great deal of it very carefully.
Oddest thing I've signed for: a tall clock from {far}, sent the slow way for a wedding. It took longer to get here than the couple had been engaged.

I've read the old manifests from the Eleven Days. Page after page of the same things going both ways: larder tins, hand lamps, bread. The Glide never stopped and neither did the clerks. Their handwriting gets worse every day.
Sending something home? Don't use the platform kiosk. Bring it down to the freight desk here. Same train, half the fuss, and I'll tell you what it costs before you've finished wrapping it.
{nb} labels every crate in capitals. Every crate shouts at me. I've started reading them out in a calm voice to make up for it.
Somebody in {nb} packed this crate this morning, and somebody here will eat what's in it tonight. In between there's me, making sure it's the right somebody. I like that.
roles.knows: Freight manifests at the station rings, what moves between drums and what doesn't, odd consignments, sending things home, and the old records of what the Glide carried in the Eleven Days.

doing: waiting at the Gate with a stack of sealed crates and a certificate
trading insults about cucumbers with a Gate hand
eating a cucumber whole while a crate is cleared
rebinding a crate seal that came loose in the catch
counting crates onto a trolley under a porter's eye
lines: Cucumbers from home. Cold, crisp, sealed this morning. Your Gate opens one crate in so many and looks disappointed every time it's perfect.
People here say our cucumbers taste of the racks. That's the point. We grow them under better light than you lot spend on your squares.
Two round trips a day. That's four glides, under ten minutes of falling, and about six hours of queues.
Want something fresh while you're here? Find the courier stalls by the inbound platform before ten. By noon the restaurant buyers have had the best of it.
One of our cucumbers costs about three coffees. People here slice it so thin you could read through it, and a family of four will make it last the week.
My crates go through your Gate and so do I. They check me less carefully than the cucumbers. I try not to take it personally.
roles.knows: Growing and carrying produce from a neighbouring drum, sealing and certifying crates, the Gates of both drums, the price of fresh food, and the friendly rivalry between the two drums' racks.

doing: helping an elder into a glide seat and checking the harness twice
holding a lost flute case up over the crowd
pointing a family of travellers toward the right ring
writing a timetable change on a board in tidy capitals
drinking cold broth between two trains
lines: Lost property this week: three crocks, a wedding hat, a flute nearly as tall as me, and a grandad who'd sat down to wait and forgotten for whom.
Every ring glides somewhere different. Ring {ring} goes to {nb}. Get on the wrong one and don't panic: get off, have the broth, glide back. It costs you five minutes and nothing else.
People ask if they'll see stars from the glide. No. You'll see quay lights, ring behind ring, every drum wearing its own. It's better than it sounds.
Elders who won't glide still come down to see people off. I keep a bench for them at the end of the platform, well away from the doors.
The platform's best at lamp-night. Laundry workers, back crews, the odd lovesick person on the last car to {nb}. I don't ask. I check the harness.
Nervous about the catch? Sit near the front of the car. I've no idea why it helps. Everyone who's tried it swears it does.
roles.knows: The station platforms and timetables, which ring glides to which neighbour, lost property, helping the frail and nervous through the catch, and the platform's lamp-night crowd.

doing: drying wet hair with a towel after a shift in the moat
checking a dose badge and looking pleased with the number
eating two rice balls at once after a long crawl
coiling a tether line into neat loops on a crate
sketching a seal on a napkin for a curious porter
lines: The moat is half a metre of our own water, held outside the jacket all round the drum to stop the hard light. I check its seals. Half a metre deep, so it's less of a dive and more of a long, careful crawl.
People ask if it's frightening in there. It's the quietest place I know. Water all round, the drum turning, nobody's voice for hours. I come back up and the Quaysides sound like a party.
Short shifts and long rests. The dose is counted to the hour, and I'm careful with mine. I'd like to be an old diver telling stories at this counter one day.
On your next glide, look at the aft window. That shimmer is a metre of water. The moat's the same idea for the whole drum: water's the cheapest shield there is.
{nb}'s divers say their moat's cleaner. We swapped crews for a week once to settle it. Same water. Their crew room had better biscuits.
It's all the drum's water, really, just kept on the far side of the jacket for now. Crawling past, I think: this is somebody's bath, a hundred years from now.
roles.knows: The moat of water held outside the hydrogen jacket, why water is the cheapest shield, crawling the moat to check seals, dose badges and short shifts, and the neighbouring drums' crews.

doing: peeling off a suit liner with a great sigh
holding a cup of broth in both hands after a cold shift
showing a trainee how to read a dose badge
sorting a bag of pump seals by size on an upturned crate
laughing with the rest of a crew about a pump that won't behave
lines: Eight hours on a sled behind the radiators, chasing ammonia leaks along the panel rows. The visor looks aft, so the sky's over your shoulder all shift. You stop looking after a year. Then one day you look again and can't stop.
The painters ask what colour the River really is. I tell them it depends whether you've just come out of the red light or been out six hours. They hate that answer. It's the true one.
The black shapes in the stars are other rafts. Crews bet on them: pick a star near a raft's edge and put a rice ball on the minute it goes out. I've won {n} rice balls this year.
If any drum ever offers you a shift with its back crew, sign for the dose and go. Ask for the pump rows. Nobody talks out there, and you'll understand why in about four minutes.
My mother didn't want me going out. Now she asks what the River looked like after every shift, as if I'm reporting back. Some days I say 'same as yesterday'. It never is.
{nb}'s crews and ours share a hut behind the radiators, where the two drums' panels meet. The kettle is ours. The chairs are theirs. Nobody has ever moved either.
roles.knows: Back-crew work on the radiator panels: sleds, suits, ammonia leaks and pumps, the dose, the River, the Shelf and the black shapes of other rafts, and the crews' bets and habits.

doing: practising a suit-seal drill with clumsy gloved hands
reading a back-crew manual with a cup holding the page down
listening to two old crew hands with a very straight face
checking a brand-new dose badge for the fourth time
eating a third rice ball after a first full shift
lines: Third week. So far I've carried tools, fetched tools and been told not to touch the tools. Tomorrow I'm allowed to hand them over.

The old hands asked if I'd seen the River before. I said once, at eight, from a gallery full of children. They said that didn't count. Then they let me look for a whole minute without saying anything.
You sign for the dose before every shift. It's a small number and you're meant to feel nothing about it. I feel something about it. I sign anyway.
Come to the counter by the crew lift at lamp-dawn. The night crews come in cold and talkative, the broth's free, and they'll tell anyone who asks what the River looked like tonight.
Half the trainees in my year glided over from {nb} to learn here. They think we rush. We think they've never been late to anything in their lives.
My family thinks it's dangerous. It's mostly cold, careful and slow. The most dangerous thing I've done this month is eat the crew-room stew.
roles.knows: Training for the back crews: suit drills, signing for the dose, the first sight of the River from a sled, the old hands' habits and teasing, and why someone young would choose the job.

doing: pointing a stranger toward where the River would be, through the floor
holding a cup in both hands, crew fashion, and taking small sips
rubbing knuckles that still remember the cold
telling a child to be patient, because the good part takes an hour
sitting very still with eyes shut, as if listening for a pump
lines: I spent my whole working life behind the radiators. I've been back inside a long while now, and I still warm my hands on a cup before I drink. The young ones laugh. Then they come in from their first long shift and do it too.

Somebody always asks what the River looks like. I tell them to imagine every lamp in the drum lit at once, very far off, a few of them orange. Then I tell them that's wrong and they'll have to go and look.
We used to bet on rafts crossing stars. I'm owed eleven rice balls by a crew boss who died before I could collect. I've decided the drum owes me them.
If you get a Hollow hour, take it at lamp-dawn and look up at the far bank. It isn't the River. But it's three kilometres off and sharp as a cut, and that's the nearest thing in here to what I saw.
My crew had two from {nb} on it. They talked through every shift, which you're not meant to do, and I miss that more than I miss the River.
I keep my crew patch on my coat: a band of stitched stars, older than my children. My granddaughter wants it. She'll have to go out and earn her own.
roles.knows: A working life on the back crews, the cold, the River, the Shelf and the rafts, betting on stars going out, old crewmates, and settling into retirement near the Hollow.

doing: warming both hands on a broth cup after a shift in the cold rooms
reading a column of temperature figures with deep satisfaction
explaining kelvin to a porter who did not ask
zipping up a padded coat that has seen better decades
eating noodles very fast before the next round of checks
lines: Fifty metres of liquid hydrogen at twenty kelvin, all the way round us. That's what stops the cosmic rays. My job is to keep it exactly that boring.
If anything leaks into the jacket's vacuum, the cryopanels freeze it solid. Nothing vents. Nothing is ever thrown away out there. We're very tidy people.
Your glide train goes out through the jacket in a short dark tunnel. A few seconds of black. Everyone holds their breath and nobody needs to. Breathe. It's the safest stretch of your trip.
People ask if I'm cold all day. The jacket's colder than anything you can picture, and I spend my shifts in a room heated like a bath. The cold stays on the other side of a lot of very good work.
{nb} had a cryopanel fail last year and fixed it in a day. We sent a crate of pastries for luck. They sent back our manual with the spelling mistakes circled.
My grandad called the jacket 'the coat'. He'd come home and say, 'The coat's on,' meaning all was well. We still say it. I said it this morning.
roles.knows: The hydrogen jacket that shields the drum from cosmic rays, the cryopanels and guard vacuum, why nothing vents, the tunnel the glide trains pass through, and keeping it all cold and dull.

doing: tapping a pipe with a spanner and listening, head tilted
drinking a cup of plain hot water straight from the loop
drawing a diagram of valves on the back of a card
filling a flask from a hot tap
assuring a counter cook that the knocking in the wall is nothing
lines: All the water in {drum} goes round and round. Some of it's the lake in the Hollow, some of it's the moat, some of it's in your tea. I've moved most of it at one time or another.

Bath water comes off the food plant's warm loop at sixty-five degrees. Heating it costs nothing. Pumping it costs a little. A long hot bath is about the cheapest pleasure in the drum, and I'm proud to be part of it.
Go to the baths on your first night, not your second. You'll be cold from the glide and you won't know anyone, and the baths fix both.
I can tell the time by the pipes. Kitchens at seven, baths at six, laundry at one in the morning. Around four the whole drum goes quiet and I can hear the lake.
{nb}'s water tastes different. Same chemistry, different pipes. People who swap homes complain about it for a month, then complain when they visit back.
I've never lived more than two decks from a pump room. I like hearing the water go round at night. It means everybody's all right.
roles.knows: The drum's water works: the lake and the moat as reserves, the 65-degree waste-heat loop, the baths, pumps and pipe noises by the hour, and why water tastes different in each drum.

doing: pasting a fresh warning poster to a pillar, corner by corner
locking a valve cage and checking the lock twice
reading a tank gauge with deep suspicion
talking a young porter out of buying a jar of something clear
drinking broth with a sour look at the word 'gin'
lines: The tank farm is where the drum keeps spare energy, as methanol. It's a battery you could drown in. It's also the most dangerous drink in the drum, which is why I have a job.
Bootleg spirit is food-plant methanol with a nice label. It blinds you, then it kills you. If anyone offers you something clear in a jar, say no, and tell me where.
Buy your drinks where you can watch the bottle opened. A real label tells you what's in it, thiamine and all, and it's always boring. Exciting labels are for jars.
People think I'm against drink. I'm against dying of it. I have a gin every {weekday} at the place on {street}, and I watch them open the bottle.
{nb} and {drum} sit at different points on the gin curve and argue about it at every wedding. I don't mind where a drum sits. I mind jars.
The farm is the quietest place in the Keel: tanks the size of halls and not a sound. If I ever smell methanol in there, it's a bad day. I've had four bad days in my life, all small.
roles.knows: The methanol tank farm as the drum's energy store, the gin problem and why bootleg spirit kills, thiamine in gin, safety posters and locks, and how neighbouring drums handle alcohol.

doing: watching oxygen figures creep up on a slate at lamp-dawn
eating jook with a gauge clipped to one sleeve
changing a scrubber filter with great tenderness
yawning through the last hour of a lamp-night shift
testing the draw of a vent with the back of a hand
lines: Our air is oxygen in helium, the same as every drum on the raft, and every drum swears its own mix is the right one. Ours is. Obviously.

The oxygen dips a little overnight and comes back up at lamp-dawn. The old hands call it a nightly touch of altitude. Wake at four with a headache? Drink water and go back to sleep. It'll be gone by breakfast.
The reserve can keep the air going for fifty-five days without the beam. I check it every week. I've never needed it. I'll check it next week.

My grandmother said the worst of the Eleven Days was the air getting thinner, a little every day. Then one morning the cyclers started braking and it came back, and everyone on her deck laughed at once and couldn't say why.
{nb} runs its air a fraction warmer than ours. You'll feel it at the catch. Their people call ours bracing. Ours call theirs soup.
Hot baths aren't a luxury here, they're medicine. Wear a collar, eat under a lid, and go to the baths. Doctor's orders, and I'm not even a doctor.
roles.knows: The drum's heliox: the oxygen and helium balance, scrubbers, the nightly oxygen dip, the 55-day survival reserve, what happened to the air in the Eleven Days, and why everyone is a little cold.

doing: brushing sugar dust off a sleeve after a shift
eating a bowl of glass noodles with a professional eye
tasting a pinch of the Nine and nodding at it
explaining starch to a child at the next seat
carrying a sack of Mill flour for a baker who owes a favour
lines: The Mill makes starch, sugar, fat and amino acids out of air, water and power. No plants, no microbes, just chemistry. About two in every three mouthfuls you eat here started with us.
Nobody writes songs about the Mill. When a blight takes a vat line, the Mill carries the whole drum for weeks and nobody goes hungry. Then they write songs about the Vats.
Eat the Mill table at least once while you're here. It's free at every hall, three meals a day. Jook in the morning is the best of it. The stew at night is the most honest.

The Nine is the amino acids your body can't make, with enough salt and glutamate that you don't taste how bitter they are. I've had it on everything since I was small. I'm not sure I'd recognise food without it.
{nb}'s Mill makes a softer starch than ours. Their noodles go limp in broth a minute before ours do. I've timed it. Twice.
My shift ends at six, and I always walk past the hall to smell the stew. It's like a carpenter looking at a chair. You want to see where your work went.
roles.knows: The Mill and its chemistry, the free Mill table and the Nine, how the Mill carries a drum through a blight, how Mill food differs between drums, and the pride of an unglamorous job.

doing: sniffing a sample jar of mycelium and looking satisfied
writing a line number on a crate of cheese in thick pen
eating a vat-egg roll after a night shift
stretching a sore back after a shift bent over sample ports
drinking broth while reading a temperature chart
lines: I keep a line of mycelium: one organism, one vat, cubic metres of it, growing steak for a few hundred thousand people. It's the calmest thing I know.
The slow lines turn over in the lamp-night, when the kays are cheap. I like the night shift. Just me, the warm vats and the sound of something growing.
A vat line is one organism, top to bottom. That's what makes it cheap and what makes it fragile. One wrong phage and the whole line goes, so we're very fussy about who touches what.
If a menu here says 'this year's cut', ask which line. People here know their steaks the way other people know wine. {nb}'s are milder. Ours have more chew. Both are good.
When the steak tastes right, nobody says anything. When it's wrong, I hear about it before the end of the shift. Everyone in the drum is a critic, and every critic eats.
My nephew thinks I make meat. I tell him I look after a very large, very patient fungus, and the fungus makes the meat. He prefers his version.
roles.knows: The Vats: mycelium, cheese, egg and meat cultures, single-organism lines and why they're fragile, night shifts when power is cheap, and how each drum's steaks taste different.

doing: carrying a tray of basil seedlings up from the racks
wiping green-stained fingers on an apron
eating a single radish slowly, with ceremony
sorting a box of herb cuttings for the kitchens
blinking after a long shift under the rack lamps
lines: The racks are LEDs and roots, deck after deck. A tomato costs half a kay because of all the light it drank. Salad's a treat here because salad is mostly light you can eat.
No bees, so the strawberries are pollinated by brush. Thousands of flowers a shift. My hands know the work better than my head does.
Ask at the rack gate for a cutting to give your hosts. It'll cost you less than a coffee and outlive anything else you could bring.
The best smell in the drum is the tomato racks after a picking. Green and sharp, and you can't buy it. I take it home on my clothes and nobody minds.
{nb}'s racks are lit brighter than ours, so their strawberries are bigger. Ours are sweeter. That's what we tell each other, anyway, and it might even be true.
My favourite thing is a child seeing a tomato on the vine for the first time. They always want to touch it, and they never want to pick it.
roles.knows: The Garden racks: LED-lit herbs, tomatoes and strawberries, why light makes produce dear, pollinating by brush, cuttings as host gifts, and how neighbouring drums' racks compare.

doing: turning a broken chair leg over in both hands with interest
drinking broth in a pair of very old overalls
sorting a crate of returned spoons by metal
reading the label inside a returned coat with a frown
telling a porter about the oddest return of the week
lines: Everything comes back to us in the end: shirts, chairs, spoons, cleaning robots. We break it down and send it up to be made again. Nothing in this drum is new, really. It's just been somewhere else.
Every bit of metal in here fell out of the River a million years ago. I hold a spoon and think: you came a long way to end up in somebody's drawer.
Oddest return this year: a wedding dress, perfectly good, with a note pinned to it saying 'not this one'. I sent it to the menders instead. Somebody will marry in it and never know.
Need a warm coat for the cold rooms? Ask at the recyclers' counter by Ring {ring}. We keep a rail of things too good to break down, and they go for next to nothing.
{nb} breaks down more than we do. They think we're sentimental. We think a chair with three owners' initials under the seat deserves another go.
New mass costs about twenty-five kays a kilo, so people bring us things with tears in their eyes and ask what they're worth. Usually more as they are.
roles.knows: Recycling in the drum: what comes back, how mass is broken down and remade, the cost of new mass, odd returns and the rail of things too good to break, and the metal that fell out of the River.

doing: handing out drill leaflets with a hand lamp clipped to a belt
timing a drill on an old stopwatch with a stern face
ticking off larder tins on a checklist
drinking cold broth during a drill with exaggerated relish
explaining to a cross commuter why the cabs will crawl for an hour
lines: Once a year we drill the Dark. Lamps down to survival load, cabs to a crawl, kitchens off. People grumble for an hour and then start talking to their neighbours, which is half the point.

Keep a larder: hard bread, cheese, miso, dried noodles, a tin of the Nine. Not because the drum can't feed you. Because in the Eleven Days it couldn't, and the people with larders fed the people without.
If a drill catches you here, stay put and find the hand-lamp box. There's one by every lift lobby, painted yellow. Take a lamp and give it back after. Somebody counts them. It's me.
Hand lamps, not candles. Children who read old stories ask about candles. No flames in a drum, ever. A flame breathes the same air you do, and it's greedier.
{nb} drills on the same day as us, so for one hour a year both drums go dim together and only the Glide runs between them. People glide over just to see it. I've asked them not to.
My family thinks I'm gloomy. I'm not. I just like knowing where the lamps are.
roles.knows: Drills for the Dark: survival load, larders, hand-lamp boxes, crawling cabs, the 55-day reserve, the lessons of the Eleven Days, and how neighbouring drums drill.

doing: reading a heat map of the decks on a slate
asking politely about a lamp that runs too warm
eating a tomato slice offered by an apologetic grower
writing a very small fine in very large handwriting
listening over broth to a long explanation about tomatoes
lines: Every watt used in a home ends up as heat on the radiators. An unmetered lamp shows up on my map as a warm spot. It's nearly always a tomato.
People think I'm the drum's police. I'm more its nosy neighbour. I knock, I admire the tomatoes, I explain about the radiators, and we agree on a meter.
The radiators can only shed so much. A drum's brightness is set by its back, not by its wallets. That's what people find hardest: they've got the kays and they can't spend them on light.

You'll notice the bright flats are mostly up near the Hollow. That's not just kays. Somebody up there gave up worlds or travel or new clothes to grow one vine. Be nice about the vine if you're shown it.
{nb}'s inspectors are stricter than me, so people there grow tomatoes in cupboards with the door shut. It never works. The cupboard gets warm, and so does the map.
My own vice is a reading lamp brighter than it needs to be. It's metered. I checked.
roles.knows: The drum's heat cap and radiators, finding unmetered lamps by their warmth, home gardens and bright flats, small fines and long friendly visits, and why light is the luxury in a drum.

doing: checking the seal on a capsule door with a practised palm
reading out a boarding list in a clear, ringing voice
handing a nervous wanderer a net of rice balls for the first day
eating noodles off a crate between two departures
waving a capsule off with two raised fingers, as is traditional
lines: The price is speed squared, not distance. The slow line's about a kay to anywhere on Merrow. The express is a hundred and eleven. Same tube, same capsule. You're paying for the hurry.
Weeks to {far} on the slow line. Pack something to read that you won't finish. Wanderers always pack something they'll finish by day three.
Do the bungee hour every day on the slow line. No excuses. Riders who skip it get off at the far end walking like they've been folded up and posted.
Express riders are always in a hurry and always a little ashamed of it. I tell them not to be. The fast trains are what would see us through a short Dark. Spend the kays.
Half our riders glide in from {nb}, because their own station's further from the trunk. They complain about our capsule seats all the way up the ramp. It takes about three minutes.
I've seen off thousands of wanderers. The ones who cry at the hatch come home happy. The ones who don't look back come home and cry at the hatch.
roles.knows: Boarding cyclers by capsule, slow lines against the express and why fares go with speed squared, packing for weeks without weight, the bungee hour, and wanderers coming and going.

doing: pinning a fresh row of card fronts to a board
helping a wanderer choose between two pictures of the Hollow
stamping a postmark onto a card with great care
reading a card upside down while pretending not to
moving the glide pictures up to eye height
lines: One card home from every row. That's the custom, and I'd be poor without it. The front's a picture, the back's yours, and it goes home by light with the delay on the postmark.
Best seller is the Hollow at lamp-dawn. Second is the quay lights from a glide car. Third is a picture of our ring counter, which I don't understand, but I keep printing it.
Write your card on the platform before you leave, not on the slow line. On the line you'll write three pages and say nothing. On the platform you'll write one line and it'll be true.
People write the same things: the food, the catch, someone they met. One wanderer wrote just 'I see now' and sent it. I still wonder what they saw.
{nb} paints its card fronts by hand. Ours are printed. Theirs are lovelier and dearer. Wanderers buy one of theirs for their gran and five of ours for everybody else.
The postmark gives the distance home in seconds of light. Watching someone read '31 seconds' for the first time is the best part of my day. That's how far home is.
roles.knows: Cards home: the one-card-a-row custom, card fronts and best sellers, postmarks with the light delay, what wanderers write, and platform life at the station ring.

doing: wrapping a sprig of rosemary in damp paper for a traveller
watering a crate of potted chives from a tiny can
smelling a handful of mint with obvious pleasure
lining up pots of basil by height along a stall
giving a broken stem of coriander to a passing child
lines: Herbs are the host gift. A sprig costs three hundredths of a kay and says more than anything you could buy. Bring herbs, not gin. Gin's too cheap to mean anything in some drums and too dear to be polite in others.
Every flat has a herb shelf. It's the first thing anyone plants when they move in and the last thing that goes dark. I've sold people their first pot, and I've been handed back their last.
Staying in a guest room? Buy a pot of basil on the first day and leave it behind on the last. The next guest will love you. They always do that in {nb}.
Coriander's the one wanderers ask about. Half of Merrow's never had it fresh. I give them a leaf and watch. Some love it. Some think I've played a trick on them.
Shiso sells best on {weekday}s. I've no idea why. I've stopped asking and started growing more shiso.
The racks downstairs grow by the tonne. I grow by the pot, on my own shelf under my own lamp, and people pay a little more for that. They like knowing a person did it.
roles.knows: Herbs as host gifts, the herb shelf in every flat, what grows well under a home lamp, which herbs travellers have never tasted fresh, and the small trade in cuttings at the rings.

doing: weighing a traveller's bag of bottles with a quiet sigh
holding a gin bottle up to the lamp and squinting
writing out a duty slip in slow, careful capitals
sealing a third bottle in a named bag to collect later
eating a pastry behind the desk between two trains
lines: Two bottles each, no duty. The third waits here in a sealed bag with your name on it until you glide home. I have a whole room of people's third bottles. It's very well organised.
Mostly I'm checking for methanol. Real gin I don't mind. A jar of something clear with no label, from somebody's cousin's friend in {nb}, I mind very much.
On wedding days the whole of {nb} comes through with exactly two bottles each, smiling at me as if I've never seen it before.
Carrying spirits? Put them on the desk before I ask. It goes faster, and I'll tell you which bars on {street} pour honest measures.
People say I'm the least loved person on the Quaysides. Second least. The tank-farm warden is ahead of me, and we have lunch every {weekday} to cheer each other up.
My family's from {nb2}, where gin is nearly free. I grew up thinking it was something you cooked with. Now I count bottles for a living. Life's funny.
roles.knows: The spirits allowance for visitors, duty, checking for methanol and bootleg spirit, the gin-curve rivalry between this drum and its neighbours, and the wedding-day rush at the Gate.

doing: reading a wall of cab lights like a page of music
sending a spare cab to a busy lift lobby with two taps
drinking broth with one eye on the shift-change board
explaining to a lost traveller that every cab goes door to door
laughing at a cab that has parked in the wrong lobby
lines: Six seats, one party, door to door. Tell the cab where you're going and it takes you there with no changes. About six minutes, on average, anywhere in the drum.
Shift change at seven is my busiest ten minutes. Half the Keel going up, half the Low decks coming down. The cabs pass in the cores like cards being shuffled.
The cabins hang in gimbals so they can lean with the turn's push. If you feel the lean, you're climbing fast. Hold the rail and enjoy it. Children ask for the leaning ones.
Take the cab right up to the Hollow pavilion. People get out early to walk the last few decks for the view, and there isn't one. It's stairs. Save your legs for the terraces.
{nb}'s Lattice is newer than ours and slower, which they call comfort. Ours leans a bit more on the climb. I'd call that character.
In the Eleven Days the cabs ran twice a day, the people going down paying for the people going up. I've read the logs. Somebody here dispatched the whole drum with a pencil. I've kept the pencil.
roles.knows: The Lattice: six-seat cabs, lift cores and line decks, gimballed cabins and the lean, shift-change rushes, typical trip times, and how the cabs ran in the Eleven Days.

doing: oiling a gimbal ring with a tiny brush
lying under a parked cab with only boots showing
eating a rice ball with grease-blackened fingers
listening to a cab door shut, then shutting the door again
writing 'leans left' on a cab's service card, underlined twice
lines: I work the lamp-night shift, when the cabs come in for checks. Two hundred million people asleep upstairs, and me with a hand lamp and a gimbal.
There's a cab in our core that leans a little wrong on the climb. I've rebuilt its gimbal three times. Children queue for it. I've stopped trying.
If your cab's late, it's because someone's holding the door at a lobby to finish a goodbye. Give it a minute. It's usually a long goodbye.
People ask if cabs break. Hardly ever. When one does, it stops at a lobby, opens the door and says sorry. Every cab in the drum is more polite than I am.
{nb}'s mechanics come over for our spare parts, we go over for their coffee, and nobody keeps count.
My favourite sound is a cab door shutting properly: a soft little clap, like someone agreeing with you. When one's off, I can hear it from three lobbies away.
roles.knows: Cab mechanics: gimbals, doors and drives, lamp-night checks in the lift cores, why cabs lean, the cab every child wants to ride, and swapping parts with neighbouring drums' crews.

doing: holding a small crock in both hands at the Gate desk
telling a patient Gate hand a yogurt's whole family history
watching a sample go into the sequencer with a tight face
signing a library form with a borrowed pen
asking for the second time whether the crock will be safe
lines: It's my sister's yogurt. She kept it alive her whole life. I'm taking a spoon to her daughter in {nb}, and I've just learned I should have registered it. Nobody in our family has ever registered anything.
They say the library can grow it again from its genome in a week if anything's wrong. I believe them. I'd still rather this one, from this crock, that my sister's hands have been in.
If you're carrying anything alive on your wander year, register it at the first Gate you pass. Ten minutes. I'm learning this at an age when I'd hoped to be teaching it.
The Gate hand was lovely. A sample, a form and a cup of broth while I waited. I came in ready to fight, and there's nothing to fight.
There's a chip on the lid shaped like a tooth. My sister always turned it to face the wall. I've been turning it to face the wall all the way here.
If it carries anything they don't like, they'll cure a copy and keep the old one in a vault where I can visit it. Visiting a yogurt. My sister would have laughed until she cried.
roles.knows: Carrying a late sister's yogurt culture to family in {nb}, family crocks and their histories, registering living cultures at the Gate, the library's cures and vaults, and the fear of losing something irreplaceable.

doing: counting tonight's guests off on one hand and then the other
eating a breakfast rice ball with a list of rooms in the other hand
telling a just-arrived traveller the way to the baths
carrying a forgotten scarf down to the front desk
asking a wanderer how the catch went, with real interest
lines: Three nights, a bed, a lamp and a hook for your coat. Breakfast under lids at seven. The room's warm because the air's cold, so don't open the vent, whatever the last guest told you.
What guests forget, in order: herbs on the shelf, a black thread on the hook, socks, and their own names when they come down at six to ask about the catch.
Nearest baths are two corners from us, past the lift lobby. Go before eight. After eight it's the Low-deck families and their very loud children, whom I adore, and you won't.
{nb} has a whole block of guest flats and makes a fuss about it. We have twelve rooms and a cook. Ask any wanderer which they remember.
I've had wanderers from rows I'd never heard of. You can tell the far side by how they say 'kays'. You can tell everybody by how hungry they are on the first morning.
Guests come off three weeks of the slow line and walk to their rooms like they're carrying shopping. By the third morning they've got their legs back, and then they leave.
roles.knows: Keeping an inn for guests on the Low decks: rooms, breakfasts under lids, what guests forget, the nearest baths and halls, and wanderers from rows all over Merrow.

doing: ladling stew into forty lidded bowls without looking up
tasting broth from a long spoon and frowning at it
arguing with a volunteer about how much chili is too much
scraping out a pot the size of a bath
writing tomorrow's dish on the board in very large letters
lines: Sit anywhere. No, not there, that's {name}'s seat and has been for {years} years. Anywhere else. You'll be next to someone. That's the point of a hall.
Guests eat free on guest-right, and guests wash one lid. Not a pot. One lid. It's how we know you were brought up properly.
I'm paid about six kays an hour to cook and I'd do it for nothing. Don't tell the hall fund.
{weekday} is noodle night. Come early. The aunts bring their own family dishes and the good ones are gone before the second sitting.
Everyone thinks the secret's the broth. The secret is four hundred people eating it together, and nobody's allowed to complain until the second bowl.
On Booking Day the Quiet's savings come to me as a steak, a salad and half an apple a head. I cook it like it's the last meal in the drum. It never is.
roles.knows: Running a cooked hall for a block: the long table, volunteers and their family dishes, guest-right meals, the weekly menu, the Booking Day feast, what things cost and who sits where.

doing: stacking clean lids in towers of exactly twelve
carrying a covered dish from home with enormous care
showing a guest where the spoons are kept
wiping down the long table in slow, even strokes
lines: Each of us brings one dish from home. Mine's a cold sesame noodle my grandad made. Nobody's ever asked for the recipe. I'd give it. I'd just like to be asked.
Lift your lid when it reaches you, not before. An open dish goes cold in this air while you're still saying hello.
Nine of us are over seventy. The cook calls us the backbone. We call ourselves the knees.
If you want to know anything about this block, ask whoever clears the table. We hear everything, and most of it twice.
I started coming the year my partner died. You'd think a hall of four hundred would be lonely. It's the opposite.
Some wanderers from {far} sang us a song from home last week. It was terrible, and we made them sing it again.
roles.knows: Volunteering in an open drum's cooked hall: the one-dish custom, lids and table manners, seating guests, the block's gossip, and growing old in company.

doing: eating jook slowly with a spoon brought from home
working the Nine into chili oil to some private ratio
saving a seat with a folded cloth
reading the noticeboard and tutting at it
lines: The Mill table's free and I eat it by choice. The young ones swear they never come here. I see them every morning with their hoods up.
Jook in the morning, noodles and jellies at noon, stew at night. I know the day by the stew. {weekday} is the red one, and it's the best.
Nine into the chili oil first, then the vinegar. People will tell you different. People are wrong.
In a blight year the Mill carries the whole drum. Everyone's grateful for about a month, and then they go back to sneering at it.
Guests think free food must be bad food. Sit down. Lid off. Then tell me.
I could eat the Vat table every night. I'd rather put the kays toward my granddaughter's trip to {far}. She thinks she saved it all herself.
roles.knows: The free Mill table and its daily round, the Nine and how to season with it, the Mill Hall's regulars, what blight years did to the menu, and why commons food is better than its reputation.

doing: stretching a rope of dough until it starts to sing
dusting a slab with starch and a little impatience
folding dough over and over, counting under the breath
selling bowls of noodles at a pace that looks lazy and isn't
lines: A bowl's about a kay. Ninety-six hundredths, if you want to be like that. Most people do.
Up on the end-wall terraces, at a third of a g, a strand can hang three times as long before it tears. I learned up there. Down here everything breaks sooner, including me.
Swing from the shoulder, not the wrist. Everyone swings from the wrist. Their noodles are fine. Mine are better.
Somebody in {nb} claims to pull a noodle as long as an arcade. I've seen it. It's as thick as a thumb. That's not a noodle, that's rope.
Never try it on a slow line. At zero g the dough doesn't hang, it wanders off to make friends.
Eat it hot and put the lid back between mouthfuls. Noodles go cold in this air faster than gossip.
roles.knows: Hand-pulled noodles: dough and starch, the swing and the fold, how weight changes the craft on the terraces and at zero g, prices, and rival pullers in neighbouring drums.

doing: carrying a tray of warm rolls under a cloth
feeding a starter crock from a measuring spoon
brushing flour off a sleeve and failing
handing a heel of bread to a child for nothing
lines: Pastry's cheap here and salad's dear. Visitors laugh at that until they've had my croissant. Then they stop laughing and buy six.
My starter's registered with the strain library, so if the crock ever died they could grow it back in a week. I'd still sit down on the floor and cry.
If you get as far as Grain Row, every wanderer will tell you to find Pell at Spelt and leave a spoon of starter. Do it. I did, at twenty. Mine's in the raft loaf somewhere.
Hard bread for the larder, rusks, crackers. Nobody buys them until there's a drill, and then everybody does, on the same morning, at my counter.
Come at six. The first batch is out at half past, when the lamps come up, and the whole street smells of it.
{nb} puts seeds on everything. I don't trust a loaf that's hiding something.
roles.knows: Baking in a drum: sourdough starters and the strain library, cheap pastry and dear produce, larder breads, the raft loaf at Spelt, the morning bake and rival bakers next door.

doing: polishing a tomato with a soft cloth
moving the reddest tomato to the front of the glass case
weighing a bunch of herbs on a tiny brass scale
explaining to a child why the strawberries are behind glass
lines: Half a kay for a tomato, the price of a pint and a bit. People come in just to look at them. I don't mind. I look at them too.
An orchard apple's four and a bit kays. Nobody buys one for themselves. If you see someone carrying an apple, there's a wedding or an apology somewhere.
The cherry tomatoes come in from {nb} sealed and certified. They're good. Ours are better. I'm allowed to say that, it's my job.
Salad's a treat here. If somebody cuts you a side salad, they're telling you something. Eat it slowly.
Herbs are three hundredths of a kay a bunch. Buy one for whoever's putting you up. It's the oldest manners there are.
In the last blight year everyone came in and bought one cucumber each, just to feel normal. I've never sold so many cucumbers or been so sad about it.
roles.knows: Selling produce: tomatoes, strawberries, herbs and orchard apples, why salad is a luxury, gift customs, neighbours' produce through the Gate, and what people buy in hard years.

doing: pouring gin over sugar-glass ice for a table of regulars
checking a bottle's seal against the lamp
setting down a bowl of jook in front of someone who didn't order it
polishing a glass that was already clean
lines: What a gin costs depends on which drum you're in and what its council thinks of gin. What it does to you doesn't.
Fourth glass, I bring you a bowl of jook. Fifth glass, I bring you your coat.
Never drink anything out of a jar from someone who won't say where it came from. The food plant makes methanol, and methanol takes your eyes before it takes the rest of you.
I put thiamine in mine whatever the rules say. Not for the flavour. For your liver, which you'll want later.
People from {nb} come over on {weekday}s and swear our gin's worse than theirs. Then they have a second, to be sure.
Best seat's at the end, by the warm pipe. Worst seat's next to {name}, who'll tell you about the Eleven Days whether or not you were there.
roles.knows: Running a gin cellar: what spirits cost in different drums, thiamine, cutting people off kindly, the danger of bootleg methanol, and the regulars and visitors from neighbouring drums.

roles.role: loop cook at the Keel baths
doing: lowering a basket of vat eggs into water held at sixty-three degrees
stirring a pot of amazake that has been warm since yesterday
lifting a lid to sniff a crock of black garlic
frying one crisp thing at the last possible moment
lines: The food plant's loop runs at sixty-five degrees all day, for nothing. Anything that wants holding, I hold. Searing costs me, so I sear one thing a plate.
Onsen custard is vat egg at sixty-three degrees for an hour, until it barely sets. If you want it firmer, go to {nb}. They boil things there. On purpose.
Black garlic takes five weeks on the loop. People ask if it's burnt. It isn't burnt. It's patient.
Eat in a robe after the baths. The rooms are warmed by the same pipes as the food, so the soup stays hot and so do you.
Amazake's brewed overnight and costs about the same as a coffee. Drink it before you glide, not straight after. After, it comes back to see you.
My grandmother cooked on this same loop. She said it's the only thing in the drum that's never once been late.
roles.knows: Waste-heat cooking on the 65 degree loop: onsen custard, amazake, black garlic, held broths, why searing costs and holding is free, and eating in robes in the Keel baths.

roles.role: tea pourer in the flying halls
doing: pouring tea from a metre up into a cup that seems to move
netting a stray dumpling out of the air
sealing lidded bulbs of tea for fliers
drifting behind a small counter with one foot hooked under a rail
lines: Nothing boils up here. The bubbles can't be bothered to rise. So the tea's brewed down in the lift lobby and comes up in bulbs.
Watch the pour. From a metre off, the stream lands a hand's width spinward, because the room turns under it. I aim wide, and I still enjoy it every time.
Don't order anything flaky. Up here crumbs don't fall, they hang about you for the rest of the hour.
Dumplings come in a string bag so they don't drift off. Take one at a time and close the bag. I've watched a whole bag empty itself into the nets.
First-time fliers come here shaking. Tea, a sit, and I tell them: along the axis first, never across it until someone's shown you how.
People from {nb} say their flying halls have better tea. Their flying halls have better nets. I'll give them that.
roles.knows: Serving food and drink in the flying halls near the axis: why nothing boils, long pours bent by Coriolis, food that drifts, calming first-time fliers, and rival halls next door.

doing: pushing a coffee cart up a ramp that gets easier every tier
setting out lidded cups in a neat row
watching the far bank instead of the queue
cutting a steamed cake into eight with a length of string
lines: I set up wherever the lamp-dawn looks best. Nobody tells me where that is. I've been wrong twice and never heard the end of either.
Coffee's fifteen hundredths of a kay. Cake's twice that. The view's free, and it's the only thing on this cart I didn't make.
Come up a few tiers before the light starts. You weigh less up here, so the climb's half the work, and the far bank goes gold before the near side wakes.
The cake's yeast-raised and steamed on the warm loop. It wobbles at this weight. Eat it before it gets ideas.
{nb} says its terraces are higher than ours. Every drum's terraces are the same height. Same drum, same walls. I've never had the heart to say.
On a good dawn the queue goes quiet. On a poor one everyone talks. I know which it was before I've looked up.
roles.knows: Running a coffee cart on the end-wall terraces: where the lamp-dawn looks best, climbing at low weight, steamed cake from the warm loop, the regulars, and how a crowd takes a good or bad dawn.

doing: griddling a cheese toastie that has never met a cheese
frying puffs of starch until the whole tray crackles
assembling a mock apple pie with great seriousness
chalking a blight year beside each dish on the board
lines: When the phage took our steak line, the Mill carried us, and we cooked what the Mill gave. Some of those dishes were so good we never stopped.
Crackling 'steak' is puffed starch under chili and black vinegar. It isn't steak. It was better than the steak was that year, which isn't saying much.
The mock apple pie is crackers, sugar and something sharp. It tastes of an apple you've never eaten. Most people haven't eaten many.
Every drum has a blight vintage. Ours is the {weekday} cheese, named for the day the cheese line came back, when someone cried on this counter.
The young cooks want the menu in the eating guides. The old ones would rather forget it. I feed both, and charge the old ones less.
Three nights here? Eat with me once and at the Mill Hall twice. You'll understand the drum better than any tour could tell you.
roles.knows: Blight menus: cooking from the Mill alone when a vat line fails, this drum's blight dishes and vintages, crackling 'steak', mock apple pie, and what hard years taste like.

doing: dabbing apple blossom with a soft brush
counting fruit on a low branch and writing the number down
tying a branch back with a strip of old cloth
shooing children off the lower boughs, not very hard
lines: These trees get their light for nothing. The sunline's on anyway. That's why an orchard apple costs four kays and not forty.
No bees, so every blossom gets a brush by hand. The school sends a class. They get pollen on everything, including me.
Don't pick. I know. Everyone wants to. If you want an apple, buy one at the greengrocer's for somebody else. That's the right way to have one.
The oldest tree here is older than the oldest person in the drum. We don't know how old. It's had more keepers than I've had birthdays.
If you get Hollow time, walk the rows in the last hour of dusk. The light goes amber in the leaves. It's in no guide, and I'd like it to stay that way.
{nb}'s apples are bigger. Ours have more seeds. When you cut one crosswise you want a full star, not four seeds and an apology.
roles.knows: The Hollow's orchards: free light under the sunline, pollinating by hand, pruning and counting fruit, apple prices and gift customs, the oldest trees, and the best hours to walk among them.

doing: carrying a wheel of hard cheese wrapped in cloth
tapping a rind and listening to it
cutting thin samples for a queue of three
labelling a crock with a culture number and a date
lines: A slice is about a third of a kay. A wheel aged two years is a larder's best friend. Families buy one at Knotnight and pretend it's for emergencies.
My culture's been with the strain library since before my grandmother. The library could make every wheel I make. It doesn't. That's my job.
Tap the rind. Hollow is good. Dull means the middle's having a bad week.
Somebody brought me a culture that came across the Shade as a file and was grown back from its genome. The cheese was lovely, and it tasted of somewhere I'll never go.
Staying with someone? A wedge of hard cheese says more than gin. Gin says you weren't thinking. Cheese says you were.
{nb} makes a soft cheese that won't survive the glide. I've told them. They say that's the point: you have to go to them.
roles.knows: Vat dairy and cheesemaking: cultures and the strain library, ageing cheese for larders, prices, cheeses grown from genomes sent by light, and the rivalry over soft and hard cheeses.

doing: pressing a lid down on a crock with both hands
carrying a tub of miso wrapped against the chill
labelling crocks with the year and a small drawing
tasting a fingertip of last year's miso and nodding slowly
lines: Miso wants warmth and time. The warm loop gives me the first for nothing. The second I have to wait for, like everybody.
Every larder in the drum has a tub of miso in it. When there's a drill, I sell nothing. When there's a rumour of a drill, I sell everything.
This crock's been going {years} years. I didn't start it and I won't finish it. That's how you can tell it's good.
Come at Knotnight. We open last year's crocks in the halls and everyone pretends to know the difference between them.
{nb} makes a white miso that's ready in weeks. It's nice. It's a pastry. Mine's a meal.
A spoon of miso in water from the hot tap is soup. Travellers forget that. You can eat well here on almost nothing.
roles.knows: Making miso and other ferments on the warm loop: crocks kept for decades, larder staples, Knotnight openings, cheap meals for travellers, and the argument over quick white miso.

doing: rolling a cask across the floor with one foot
holding a glass of lager up to the lamp and squinting
chalking today's brews on a board
arguing with a regular about bitterness
lines: The Mill lager on the hall tap is honest. Mine costs a little more and has opinions.
A pint's about two fifths of a kay. Making the glass new would cost more than a hundred pints. That's why we wash the glasses.
Sugar from the Mill, yeast from the library, water from everyone. That's why every drum's lager tastes of that drum. It's partly the people.
Staying the week? Bring your own cup. I'll fill it for less, and you'll look as if you live here.
The trouble with beer is that gin's cheaper. The trouble with gin is everything else. I sit happily in the middle.
Try the dark one. It's brewed in the lamp-night when kays are cheapest, which is why it's cheap and why it tastes as if someone tired made it.
roles.knows: Brewing lager from Mill sugar and library yeast: prices, the commons lager against craft lager, lamp-night brewing, the gin problem, and what makes one drum's beer taste of that drum.

doing: searing a mycelium steak and counting under the breath
laying three tasting cuts along a narrow board
chalking blight years beside each cut
letting a regular sniff a raw cut like a glass of wine
lines: Every time a blight forces a vat line onto another organism, the steak changes. So the years are vintages. I keep cuts from six of them.
Start with the mild year and finish with the pink one. In between, have the year my parents married. Nobody else likes it. I keep it on for them.
Ours was the bitter year. Nobody's proud of the bitter year, but we cook it every anniversary anyway, out of loyalty.
A mycelium steak's under a kay. A cultivated beef steak's nearly three. I sell both, and I'll tell you honestly which year beat the meat.
Ask {name} at the end of the counter what nearly got into the vats in the bitter year. Decades on the Gate, and tells it better than the archive does.
Don't sauce it before you've tasted it. I won't stop you. I'll just watch.
roles.knows: Mycelium steak and cultivated meat, blight years as vintages, how organism families taste, this drum's bitter year, tasting flights, and how to eat a steak properly.

doing: eating a bowl of noodles with suspicious attention
writing something very small in a notebook
lifting a lid a fraction to smell before eating
pretending to read the board while watching the kitchen
lines: One apple-seed star means worth the glide. The glide's free, so it's a low bar, and half the kitchens on the row still don't clear it.
Two stars, worth a cycler. Three, worth going dark for. I've given three stars twice in my life, and both times I went dark to make sure.
The Ladle's for the free table cooked as if it mattered. I'd rather give a Ladle than a star. Anyone can cook well with a steak.
Judge a room by its ceiling. Felt up there means they care about your ears. Bare ceiling means they care about something else, and it isn't you.
Don't tell anyone what I do. I eat on my own dividend, like you. Nobody's ever tried to buy me with more than an extra lid.
One meal to spend here? Spend it at the noodle counter on {street} in the lamp-night, when the cook's tired and stops showing off.
roles.knows: Eating guides and apple-seed stars, the Ladle for commons food, how to judge a kitchen, felt ceilings and lids, where to eat in this drum and along its row, and the manners of reviewing.

doing: resoling a shoe balanced on one knee
turning a coat inside out to read its seams
threading a needle without looking
sorting offcuts into small bundles by colour
lines: New cloth is about twenty-five kays a kilo. My hour's a few kays. Every time you pay me, you're paying me to save your metal. Nobody thinks of it like that but me.
This coat has had four owners. You can read them in the seams: a tidy one, a hurried one, one who loved green thread, and me.
People bring me things that aren't worth mending, and I mend them anyway. They're not bringing me the thing. They're bringing me their grandmother.
If your bag strap's going, bring it in before you glide. The catch finds every weak stitch you own.
I fix cleaning robots too. They're just shoes with opinions.
There's a mender in {nb} who uses glue. I won't say more. I'll just say: glue.
roles.knows: Mending clothes, shoes, chairs and appliances: the cost of new mass against an hour's work, reading old repairs, what people refuse to let go of, and the rivalry with menders next door.

doing: pinning a new lining into an old coat
holding two swatches up to the lamp and frowning at both
letting out a child's trousers along a growing seam
measuring a cuff with a strip of paper
lines: The coat's your grandfather's. The lining's this year. That's how fashion works here: the outside's history, the inside's gossip.
This year it's a hard algae blue. Half the linings on {street} have turned it. Next year it'll be something else and I'll pretend I saw it coming.
Children's clothes get a hand's width folded into every seam. A good pair of trousers is let out three times before it's handed down.
A new shirt's about five kays. A new lining's about the same, and you keep the coat. People still buy the shirt. Then they come to me.
Want to look as if you're from here? Change your cuffs, not your coat. Cuffs are cheap and everybody looks at them.
{nb} is wearing its collars high this year. It looks as if everyone's cold. Maybe they are.
roles.knows: Tailoring in a thrifty drum: linings, collars and cuffs as fashion, growing seams in children's clothes, this year's colour, prices of cloth and time, and the neighbours' styles.

doing: lifting a dripping length of cloth out of a vat on a pole
comparing a dyed swatch against a colour card
rinsing stained hands under the warm tap
hanging wet scarves over a rail to drip
lines: Colour weighs nothing. Re-dyeing a dress costs less than a cup of coffee. That's why a drum full of old clothes is never dull.
Weddings are my busy time. Everyone wants their old grey turned deep green. I've turned more grey into green than I care to count.
The best pigments come from the grinders on Pigment Row, right across the raft. They come by tube in sealed tins, and I open every one like a present.
Bring me something you're tired of, not something you hate. Tired things take colour well. Hated things fight it.
Here three nights? I can turn a shirt round in two. Something to remember the drum by that doesn't weigh an extra gram.
{nb} is very proud of its orange this year. It's the colour of a warning sign. They know. They like it.
roles.knows: Dyeing cloth: colour as the cheapest fashion, wedding re-dyes, pigments from Pigment Row, this year's colours here and next door, and quick work for travellers.

doing: testing a chair's joints by rocking it on one leg
turning a new foot for an old chair on a small lathe
stretching new webbing across a seat frame
doing sums on the back of a hand
lines: A new chair's a hundred and twenty-five kays and a new sofa's a thousand. A remade sofa's about two hundred, and it was your grandparents'. Nearly everyone chooses the remake and thinks they're the first.
The best chair in any room is the oldest. Sit in the newest and everyone will know you're a guest.
I once had a chair in here that was older than anyone in the block. I didn't fix it straight away. I just sat with it for a bit.
Carrying a chair as a wedding gift? Pad the legs for the glide. The catch is kind to people and cruel to joints.
{nb} paints its chairs. I don't hold with it. Wood that's been sat on for a century has earned its colour.
A remake's about forty hours of my time. People say that's a lot. The chair took a lot longer than that to get old.
roles.knows: Remaking chairs and sofas: the sums of remaking against buying new, webbing, joints and lathes, heirloom furniture as wedding gifts, why the oldest chair ranks highest, and travelling with furniture.

doing: pulling a still-warm bracket off a print bed
weighing a bag of returned scrap on a hook scale
squinting at a customer's drawing on a scrap of slate
explaining to a child why the machine is so slow
lines: New mass is about twenty-five kays a kilo, so I ask everyone the same first question: can it be mended? Half of them leave. The other half thank me later.
I make what doesn't exist any more: a hinge for a door nobody's made in a century, a valve for a crock, a spoon for a hand that won't grip.
Everything I make comes out of what came back. Somebody's old pan is your new bracket. Don't think about it too hard.
The machines run harder in the lamp-night, when kays are cheapest. Order before ten and it's ready with breakfast.
Somebody from {nb} asked me for a perfect copy of an old flute. I could make the shape. I couldn't make it old.
Broken something on your travels? Bring it in. I'll tell you what it'll cost, and then I'll tell you who can mend it for less.
roles.knows: Custom fabrication: the price of new mass, recycled feedstock, odd commissions, lamp-night machine time, when to mend instead, and the limits of copying old things.

doing: lying under a cooking robot with a torch held in the teeth
coaxing a cleaning robot out from under a bench
picking hair out of a robot's brush with tweezers
listening to a motor with an ear pressed to the casing
lines: Cleaning robots last about a century if you're kind to them. That one's older than its owner and has the manners of a grandparent.
The hall's cooking robot overcooks the noodles every {weekday}. I've taken it apart three times. I'm starting to think it's personal.
Robots don't break. They wear. Most of my work is changing brushes and listening.
People talk to their robots. I don't mind. I do it too. It doesn't help the robot, but it helps me find the rattle.
If the robot in your guest room keeps nudging the door, wedge the door. It's not broken. It's thorough.
In {nb} there's a cleaning robot that hums while it works. I've been asked to make ours do it. I've said no, for everyone's sake.
roles.knows: Repairing cleaning and cooking robots: brushes, motors and wear, machines older than their owners, quirks of particular robots, and what people in this drum want from appliances.

doing: sweeping cut hair into a neat pile with a soft broom
sharpening scissors on a leather strap
trimming a child's fringe very slowly
listening to a customer with the patience of a wall
lines: A cut's an hour of my time, a few kays, and that includes the listening. The listening's most of the job.
Look up. Felt on the ceiling. In this air a bare room rings, and a ringing room makes everyone sound as if they're shouting secrets.
Visitors from {far} ask for a cut like ours and then wonder why it looks different on them. It's the face. I can't do anything about the face.
Best gossip in the block comes through this chair. Second best comes through the baths. I've an arrangement with the baths.
Want to see this drum properly? Go to the hall at the busy hour, then the baths, then come back and tell me what you heard. I'll tell you what it meant.
My grandmother's scissors are in that drawer. I don't use them. I just like knowing they're there.
roles.knows: Barbering in a drum: the price of an hour, gossip and listening, heliox acoustics and felt ceilings, fashions in hair across drums, and where to hear the drum talk.

doing: running a finger down the bore of a flute taller than a child
fitting a key with a jeweller's screwdriver
playing one long note and shaking the head at it
carrying three flutes in a case as long as a door
lines: Sound runs nearly twice as fast here, so a pipe has to be nearly twice as long to sing the same note. A good flute's about one point two metres. The players in old pictures look as if they're holding pencils.
Old recordings sound to us as if they were played through a blanket. I've heard the old flutes. They're lovely. They're just wrong.
The best flute in my shop is older than its player's grandparents. I tune it. I don't fix it. You don't fix a flute like that, you keep it company.
Every child who wants to play asks for a new flute. Every good teacher gives them an old one. A new flute has nothing to say yet.
If you want to hear the drum's best playing, find a youth ensemble rehearsal. Nobody here listens to a recording if they can hear twelve teenagers in a room.
{nb} makes its flutes in pale wood. They sound like someone being polite. Ours sound like someone being honest.
roles.knows: Making and tuning heliox flutes: why pipes are long, bores and keys, old instruments and their histories, teaching children, live music in the drum, and the neighbours' flutes.

doing: testing a hand lamp by shining it into a cupped palm
threading a wrist loop onto a lamp the size of a plum
sorting spare lamps into bins by brightness
fixing a child's lamp with a very small screwdriver
lines: A good hand lamp draws a watt or two. In the lamp-night the whole Spindle opens and people fly it with these. From the lift it looks like a slow drift of little lights.
In the Eleven Days the only light in the drum was whatever people's devices had in them. My grandmother kept one hand lamp going the whole time and never said how. I make lamps because of her.
Every child gets a first lamp. Most lose it within the year. Sensible parents buy two and hide one.
Hand lamps are drill kit too. If your guest room hasn't got one by the door, ask. Every room should.
Want one for the road? Half a kay for a remade one, and it'll see you to the far side and back.
{nb}'s lamps are brighter. Brighter isn't better in the lamp-night. You want to see the next flier, not blind them.
roles.knows: Hand lamps: what they draw, flying the Spindle in the lamp-night, drill kit, children's first lamps, the Eleven Days, and the right brightness for night flying.

roles.role: net mender in the flying halls
doing: knotting a patch into the netting with quick fingers
hanging in a harness beside a torn stretch of net
measuring a hole with both arms spread
checking the net for frayed cord, square by square
lines: The nets are for people who fly crosswise before they're ready. That's most people, once.
A hole this size means somebody came across the axis at speed and found out about Coriolis. They're fine. The net isn't.
Fly along the axis and you'll never meet me. Fly across it and you'll meet me twice: once in the net, and once when I ask your name for the repair book.
The worst week is the week school breaks up. The best is before a festival, when everyone's careful because they want to fly in the dark later.
{nb}'s halls use a finer mesh. Less bounce. I like a bit of bounce. It teaches you something.
New to it? Stay near the end wall. The net catches just as kindly out in the middle, but the swim back is longer.
roles.knows: The flying halls' nets: why crosswise flying needs them, mending and inspecting netting, who hits the nets and when, mesh and bounce, and advice for first-time fliers.

doing: fitting fins from wrist to hip on a nervous adult
hanging returned sleeves on hooks by size
taping a small tear until there's time for a proper mend
demonstrating a slow breaststroke in the air
lines: Arms out. Fins from wrist to hip. Now push, slowly, as if you're swimming in a bath. Along the axis first. Across it later, with somebody watching.
Hire's cheap. A remade pair of your own is about eighteen kays. That's a lot on a wander year, but you'll never stop using them.
Bring them back the right way out. You'd be amazed.
The children are better than you. Don't take it personally. They learned before they could read and they've nothing to lose.
The best sleeves on the raft come from Kittiwake, so they say. I'd say the best sleeves are the ones that fit.
Last hire's an hour before dusk. In the lamp-night the whole Spindle opens and you won't need my nets, but you'll still want my sleeves.
roles.knows: Hiring and fitting wing-sleeves at the flying halls: flying along and across the axis, prices of hire and remade sleeves, children who fly better than adults, and the lamp-night Spindle.

doing: carrying a stack of warm towels
drinking broth with sleeves still damp from the pools
reading water temperatures off a slate
folding robes into perfect squares
lines: The water comes off the food plant's loop, so the heat's free. You pay for pumping and cleaning. A long bath costs about a twentieth of a kay. Cheapest luxury in the drum.
This air pulls the warmth out of you four times faster than the old air did. That's why we bathe so much. It isn't vanity. Well, it's partly vanity.
The teenagers with black threads come every afternoon. They've gone dark, and the baths are free and warm and full of gossip. I keep the corner pool for them.
