Best hour's mid-morning, after the night shift's gone home and before the elders' afternoon. Bring a towel and an opinion.
Steam carries news faster than any message. If something happened in {drum} today, it was in my pools by noon.
People from {nb} glide over for our baths and say theirs are hotter. Then they stay three hours.
roles.knows: Running the baths: free heat from the food plant's loop, why heliox makes hot water a necessity, the best hours, who bathes when, gossip in the steam, and rival baths next door.

doing: waiting at the cab doors with a bag of tools
eating a rice ball between two call-outs
listening to a lift core with an ear to the wall
writing a fault on a slate in tiny letters
lines: From the rim to the top decks you lose about half your weight in a minute and a half. Good lifts make you forget that. Bad ones make you remember lunch.
The cabins hang in gimbals so they lean with the push. If your cab doesn't lean, call me. If it leans too far, call me faster.
There's a lift on deck {deck} that sings a note on the way up. The whole block knows the note. I could fix it. They'd never forgive me.
The rush is shift change. Go at ten past and you'll have a cab to yourself.
{nb} uses a different gimbal. Smoother, they say. Smoother means you don't feel the drum turning. I like to feel the drum.
The stairs are there. Walk them once, so you know why we're proud of the lifts.
roles.knows: Lift cores and cabs: gimbals and the Coriolis lean, weight changing on the climb, maintenance, the morning rush, quirks of particular lifts, and why nobody walks the stairs.

doing: timing a passing cab with a pocket watch out of habit
telling a younger engineer how it used to be done
sitting very straight with a cane across the knees
pointing out a lift core to a child and naming its age
lines: Fifty years on the cores. I can hear a bad bearing from the next block. It isn't a gift. It's the only thing my ears were ever trained for.
A young couple in {block} have asked if they can name their first child for me, when my share comes free. I said yes, but to give the child something shorter.
My old teacher worked the cores through the Eleven Days. Two trips a day, the riders going down paying for the riders going up. I trained on that same core. It still pulls a little to the left.
I live up near the Hollow now. Lighter steps. I fall over more slowly. It's the drum's way of apologising for my knees.
Want to see a good lift? Ride the core on {street} at lamp-dawn. Nobody's on it. Watch the indicator and count the decks under your breath. It's better than most music.
Don't tell me machines haven't got character. I've known lifts with better manners than councillors.
roles.knows: A long career on the lift cores: bearings and gimbals, the Eleven Days as older engineers told it, living near the Hollow in old age, being named for, and the quirks of the drum's lifts.

doing: counting empty crocks into a crate and losing count
checking a list of who's bringing what
carrying a box of hand lamps for the evening
persuading someone to bring a second jar of pickle
lines: Once a year the lamps go down and the whole block makes its larder together, like the old ring-era winters. We pickle, we press, we argue. Nobody's needed the larder in a long while. That isn't the point.
The youngest are allowed to seal the jars. The second youngest are allowed to complain that they used to seal the jars.
Every household keeps a larder: hard bread, aged cheese, miso, dried noodles, a tin of the Nine. If yours is thin, nobody says so. They just bring you an extra jar.
If you're here for Knotnight, come. Guests sit nearest the warm pipes and get the first taste of last year's pickle, which is either an honour or a test.
{nb} keeps Knotnight with music. We keep it with silence for the first hour, and then music. The silence is the bit people remember.
Every year I end the night with eleven lids too many and one jar short. I've stopped trying to understand it.
roles.knows: Organising Knotnight: the lamps going down, making the larder together, preserves and crocks, guests on the night, larder pride and what a household keeps, and how the neighbours keep it.

doing: sketching a dawn in coloured chalk on a slate
timing the sunline's ramp with a stopwatch and a scowl
arguing with an engineer about the exact shade of rose
sitting very still on a terrace step, eyes on the far bank
lines: A great dawn costs exactly what a bad one does. Same watts, same three hours. All you spend is a year of your life getting the colours in the right order.
Tomorrow's dawn is {painter}'s. If you've a terrace seat, take it. If you haven't, the lake path's nearly as good and you can lie down.
Everyone ends on white. You have to, it's morning. The art's in the hour before, while the far bank is still deciding what colour it is.
The trouble with the middle of a dawn is that people stop watching. They've seen the start and they know how it ends. The middle's where you have to be cleverest.
{nb}'s painters go bright and fast. It's like being shouted awake. Ours start slow. You're meant to wake up with the drum, not because of it.
Don't clap at the end. Clap at the moment it turns. The painters notice who claps when.
roles.knows: Light-painting: composing the Hollow's dawns and dusks, colour and timing on a fixed power budget, the painters here and next door, where to watch from, and how audiences behave.

doing: checking a light meter held at arm's length
logging dawn timings on a slate with gloved fingers
squinting up the axis through dark glasses
carrying a coil of cable toward the Spindle lift
lines: The line runs down the middle of the drum and stops about four hundred and fifty metres short of each end wall. That gap is where the flying halls are. Fly too close to the lit part at noon and you'll know about it for a week.
Three hours up, six hours full, three hours down. At full it's a hundred thousand lux on the floor. Don't look at it. Everybody tries once.
We change segments in the lamp-night, when the line's dark. People flying the Spindle wave their lamps at us. It's the friendliest work I've ever had.
I keep the line. I don't choose what it does at dawn. Whoever chooses gets the applause, and I get the complaints. That's fair. Somebody has to.
{nb} keeps its line at full for longer than we do. Ours could manage it. It isn't the line that decides, it's the budget.
Watch the first twenty minutes of dawn from the end-wall terraces. You can see the line wake up along its whole length, like somebody stretching.
roles.knows: The sunline along the drum's axis: the three-hour ramps and six-hour noon, brightness and heat near the line, why it stops short of the end walls, lamp-night maintenance, and what extra hours cost.

doing: hooking a lost sandal out of the shallows with a long pole
chalking the water temperature on a board by the jetty
whistling at a child who is about to dive
walking the shoreline with a bag of found things
lines: The lake's part of the drum's water reserve, so swim in it, don't wash in it. There's a difference, and I'll explain it if I have to.
A dive off the jetty hangs at this weight. You've time to change your mind on the way down. Don't. That's how people land flat.
The waves come in slow and tall here. Children think it's magic. It's half a g. I still think it's a bit magic.
Best swim is at lamp-dawn, when the water's still and the far bank is upside down in it and right way up above you. You can't tell which way you're floating.
Lost property this month: forty-one sandals, nine towels, a flute, and somebody's whole picnic with the lid still on.
{nb}'s lake has a sandy edge and they won't stop talking about it. We have reeds. Reeds are better for sitting in and worse for finding sandals.
roles.knows: The Hollow lake: water-reserve rules, swimming and diving at half a g, slow tall waves, safety, the best hours to swim, lost property, and the neighbours' lakes.

doing: holding a learner's ankle and letting go a little at a time
drawing a curved arrow in the air with one finger
calling out angles across the netting
untangling a learner from the net with great patience
lines: Along the axis you fly straight. Across it, the drum turns under you and you come out somewhere you didn't aim. So you aim wide. Think of it as being polite to the drum.
Nine-year-olds learn in an afternoon. Adults take a week, because adults think they know where up is.
Push slowly and glide long. Most people kick as if they're swimming at the rim, and then they meet the end-wall net sooner than they'd planned.
Book the first lesson after the flying halls open, when the nets have just been checked and nobody's showing off yet.
Crosswise lessons are on {weekday}s. Come out of a crosswise run within an arm's length of where you aimed and I'll buy you a tea.
Kittiwake children fly crosswise before they can read. I've met some. They're unbearable, and they're right.
roles.knows: Teaching flight in the flying halls: wing-sleeves, flying along and across the axis, Coriolis drift and aiming wide, nets and safety, how children and adults learn differently, and the best hours to fly.

doing: throwing a ball antispinward and watching it sail
drawing angles on a slate for a ring of children
blowing a whistle and immediately regretting it
collecting balls into a net bag
lines: Axis flies true, spin sinks, anti floats. Every child in the drum can say it. About one in ten can play it.
Throw spinward hard and the ball gains weight and dives. Throw anti and it loses weight and sails. The small ones throw anti and win. Size doesn't matter here. Angles do.
The best spinball's in the long halls on the Low decks, near full weight, where the ball really bites. Up on the terraces it's a different game and nobody agrees on the rules.
{nb}'s team throws everything along the axis. Straight and dull. We beat them every year and they never change. I'd miss them if they did.
There's a match most {weekday}s after school. Stand at the spinward end. That's where the balls go to die.
I tell the parents that bones grow best near full weight. I don't know if it's true. It gets the children to practise.
roles.knows: Spinball: the rule of axis, spin and anti, throwing angles and Coriolis, coaching children, where and when matches are played, and the long rivalry with the neighbours' teams.

doing: clapping out a rhythm for a ring of leaping dancers
calling the next figure in a voice that carries three tiers
showing a guest how to land a leap without falling over
drinking water between reels, out of breath and pleased
lines: Every leap at a third of a g comes down a hand's width spinward, so the whole reel works its way round the terrace. By the end of the night everyone's somewhere else, and so's the band.
Don't jump high. Everyone jumps high the first time. Jump long and soft, and land with your knees ready.
We dance on {weekday} nights on the third-g terrace. Guests are welcome. Guests who can't dance are especially welcome. They make the rest of us look good.
My aunts taught me the calls. I've changed three of them, and two of my aunts have forgiven me.
{nb}'s reels go antispinward on purpose, so the dancers fight the drum all night. It looks brave. It's mostly sore.
The best reels are on festival nights, with the Hollow dark and the terrace lamps low, when you can hear the dancers land all round the wall.
roles.knows: Low-gravity reels on the end-wall terraces: leaping and landing at a third of a g, why dances drift spinward, calling the figures, teaching guests, festival nights, and the neighbours' style.

doing: staking a bean vine that leans the wrong way
watering a bed from a can that feels half empty
kneeling on a pad to weed between strawberries
lifting a full sack of compost with one hand
lines: Every tier up, you weigh a little less. On the top terraces a child can jump the height of a house. I'm not allowed to. I've been asked not to.
Plants grow taller up here and weaker in the stem. I stake everything. The beans think they're trees.
The terraces get the sunline's light for free, same as the Hollow floor, so the beds are fought over. Some have been in one family for longer than anyone can remember.
Climb at lamp-dawn. You'll be light on your feet by the fourth tier, and the far bank will be going gold above you.
Strawberries up here come smaller and sweeter. Nobody knows why. I have a theory, and it involves moods.
{nb} lets its terraces run wild. Lovely to look at. Impossible to eat.
roles.knows: Gardening on the end-wall terraces: plants at low weight, free light from the sunline, who keeps which beds, strawberries and beans, climbing the tiers, and the neighbours' wilder terraces.

roles.role: elder out for the lake at lamp-dawn
doing: sitting on the elders' bench with a flask of tea
walking the lake path very slowly with a stick
watching the far bank light up, hands folded
breaking a rusk into pieces and eating each one slowly
lines: Same bench every morning, for longer than you've been alive. The bench and I have an understanding. It doesn't get up and I don't sit anywhere else.
Watch the far bank. It goes gold before we do. For about twenty minutes everyone over there is lit and we're still in the dark, and you can watch them waking up upside down.
{name} used to sit on the end of the bench, and died last year. We leave that end empty until somebody new is old enough.
In the Eleven Days the sunline went out. Somebody carried a lamp up here and we all stood at the edge to check the lake was still there. I put my hand in it to be sure.
Guests who want lamp-dawn at the lake should come quietly and sit on the grass, not the bench. The bench is spoken for. The grass is generous.
I'm told {nb} has a better lake. I'm far too old to go and find out, and I wouldn't believe it anyway.
roles.knows: Mornings at the Hollow lake: the elders' bench and its unwritten rules, lamp-dawn on the far bank, the Eleven Days remembered, friends gone, and where a guest should sit.

doing: carrying a folded chilling tent under one arm
counting this year's pears into a basket, twice
drinking tea with pollen still on the cuffs
showing a child how to hold a pollen brush
lines: Pears need a winter, and nothing here has one. So every year we wrap the trees in chilled tents for six weeks, unwrap them, and they bloom as if they've been through something.
No bees, so the school's youngest class does it with paintbrushes. Last year one child did a whole tree and then, very carefully, the bench.
The first two pears go to the oldest person in the block and the newest baby. The rest go round by lottery. I've never won. I've never minded.
The people on the upper terraces of the atrium say the pears get more light than they do. They're right. I don't bring it up.
If you're here while the pears are in blossom, come and look. It lasts about ten days, and it's the only thing in the drum that has a time of year.
A block in {nb} grows cherries. Cherries need a winter too. We lend each other tents.
roles.knows: Keeping a block's espaliered pear trees: chilled tents to give them a winter, hand pollination by schoolchildren, the pear lottery, arguments over the atrium's light, blossom time, and the neighbours' fruit.

doing: rehearsing short vows under the breath
wiping an apple knife on a clean cloth
checking a seating plan against a list of who isn't speaking to whom
straightening a couple's collars with brisk hands
lines: Short vows. The long ones never mean more, and in this air everyone can hear you anyway.
Then I cut the apple crosswise and lift the halves so everyone sees the star of seeds. For most people here it's the only star they'll ever see. My hand still shakes every time.
Weddings are best on the third-g terraces. The dancing's better and the old people can stand longer. Nobody faints at a third of a g. They just sit down slowly.
The couple eat half the apple each and everyone else watches. It's the dearest food at the wedding and it's gone in four bites.
Invited to a wedding here? Bring herbs from a shelf, or nothing. Not gin. Gin says you came for the party.
Last month I married a couple from here and {nb}. Two families who'd argued about broth for {years} years. They argued at the wedding too. It was lovely.
roles.knows: Officiating weddings: short vows, the apple cut crosswise to show its star, terrace weddings at a third of a g, gifts and manners, and families from neighbouring drums.

doing: carrying a re-dyed dress in a padded bag
counting chairs under the breath
pinning a sprig of herbs to a stranger's collar
checking a list, folding it, unfolding it, checking it again
lines: My niece is marrying a lad from {nb}. His family's bringing a new sofa, because that's what they do over there. We're bringing her grandmother's, remade. We'll see which one she sits on.
Everyone wears what they have, altered. My dress was grey for twenty years. Now it's green. It cost less than a cup of coffee and I feel like somebody new.
Come if you like. Weddings here are loud, the dancing's worse than it looks, and there's always too much food. Bring a sprig of something green.
The apple's the dearest thing on the table. I've told the children they get to watch it cut, not eat it. They've told me that's cruel. They're right.
I stood at her naming. I'm allowed to cry first, and I intend to.
The groom's family comes in on the {weekday} glide. If thirty nervous people get off one car carrying a sofa, that's them.
roles.knows: Family weddings: altered and re-dyed clothes, remade furniture against new, gifts and guest manners, the apple, families from neighbouring drums, and keeping a big day on its feet.

doing: holding a wrapped gift very still
straightening a jacket that is clearly borrowed
retying a ribbon on a small box of seeds
practising a toast under the breath
lines: My cousin's marrying into {drum}. I've glided over for the day. The catch nearly took the present out of my hands. It's a bowl. It's fine. I think it's fine.
Where I come from we give new things at weddings. Here they give old things, remade. I've been warned to admire the chair and not ask how old it is. I'm going to ask.
Is this the way to the end-wall terraces? My cousin said follow the music. I can hear four kinds of music.
I've brought herbs off my own shelf for the host. My mother said it's the oldest manners there are. She also said don't drink anything I can't see poured.
The last glide home's at one in the morning. If I miss it I'm sleeping on somebody's floor, and that somebody might be you.
Weddings at a third of a g are mostly leaping. I've been practising on my bed. The bed lost.
roles.knows: Being a wedding guest from a neighbouring drum: the glide over with a gift, how wedding customs differ between drums, herbs as a host gift, the late glide home, and dancing at low weight.

doing: counting eight-year-olds onto the Spindle lift with a clicker
holding an elbow steady at the lift door
checking a list of names for the next round
explaining zero g to a small, serious face
lines: Before the shutter opens, everyone sits in red light for twenty minutes so their eyes can wake up. The children hate it. Then the shutter opens and they understand.
No near stars. There haven't been for longer than anyone can count. What you see is the River, a broad band of pale gold frayed at the edges with dust, and the Shelf, fainter, above and below it.
The black shapes where nothing shines are rafts. Some our size, some far bigger. About a sixth of the sky is rafts. The children always ask whether anyone's looking back. I say probably.
Every child comes once, at about eight, with one adult of their choosing. They choose years ahead. I've seen children bring a grandparent, a teacher, and once the lift engineer from their block.
{nb} keeps no Window, so their children come to ours. We don't charge. We do make them sit in the red light like everyone else.
The question I get most is where the metal comes from. I point at the River. Every chair, every spoon, every bone in that child's hand fell in from out there over a million years.
roles.knows: Guiding children at the Window: dark adaptation in red light, the River, the Shelf and the dust lanes, rafts as black shapes against the stars, where the metal comes from, and what eight-year-olds ask.

roles.role: eight-year-old on the way to the Window with a grandparent
doing: holding a grandparent's sleeve with both hands
bouncing on tiptoe in the queue for the Spindle lift
counting the terraces out loud on the way up
asking the same question for the fourth time
lines: I'm going to see the stars. Real ones. Not the apple. I chose Gran when I was four and Gran said yes before I'd finished asking.
You have to sit in red light for twenty minutes first so your eyes wake up. I've been practising with my eyes shut. It's very boring.
Gran says there's a River and it isn't water. It's stars all squashed together. I don't believe it but I'm going to check.
Did you go to a Window when you were eight? Was it good? Don't tell me. Yes, tell me. No, don't.
My friend in {nb} hasn't been yet, so I'm going to tell him everything. I might make some of it up, but only the boring bits.
At the top of the lift you don't weigh anything. Gran says hold on to her and not the walls. Gran used to work out there, so Gran knows.
roles.knows: Being eight and about to see the sky for the first time: the Window trip, the red-light wait, what grandparents have said about the River, friends who haven't been yet, and very big feelings.

doing: copying a melody onto ruled paper with great care
humming one phrase over and over, changing a single note
carrying a bound songbook wrapped in cloth
explaining light delay to a doubtful choir member
lines: Every few years another raft passes close, about a quarter of an hour away by light, and we sing to it. You send a song, wait more than half an hour, and theirs begins. It's the longest rest in music.
I keep the book of what we've traded: {years} years of songs from rafts we'll never be near again. Some we still sing, and nobody remembers which ones were ours.
When Selkie passed, Carillon sang to it, and Selkie sent back a round sung against itself. Every choir on the raft has tried to copy it since. Nobody's managed.
Their voices sound nearly like ours. A little different in the vowels. You can hear a whole other history in about four bars.
If a raft's passing while you're here, go to any hall in the evening. Somebody will be singing to it, and somebody will be crying in the gap.
The kitchens trade too. We sent our {weekday} stew once. They sent back a dish with seven spices we'd never had, and the library grew three of them from the genomes.
roles.knows: The Passing and its songs: singing across the light delay to a passing raft, the songbook of traded music, Carillon and Selkie, recipe trades, and what other rafts' voices sound like.

doing: conducting a hummed phrase with one finger
pinning a rehearsal rota to a board
holding a tuning pipe up to one ear
telling the altos, kindly, that the entry was early
lines: In this air voices keep their pitch but brighten. Everything sounds as if it's sung at lamp-noon. My job is to make it sound like dusk sometimes.
Felt on the walls, felt on the ceiling, and still the room rings. A choir in a bare hall is like singing inside a bell. Lovely for a minute. Then you want to lie down.
Rehearsal's {weekday} at seven. Visitors can sit at the back. If you can hold a note, I'll put you in the middle where nobody can hear you.
The hard part of a choir isn't the music. It's who stands next to whom. I've moved {name} four times this year and it's still not right.
{nb}'s choir sings faster than ours. They call it energy. I think they're trying to reach the end before something goes wrong.
Recordings are perfect and free and nobody comes to hear them. Forty people in a room making mistakes together, and the hall's full. I've never understood it and I'd never change it.
roles.knows: Leading a heliox choir: how voices sound in heliox, acoustics and felt, rehearsals and the politics of seating, visitors who want to sing, and why people still come to hear live music.

doing: humming a part quietly while waiting for a cup of broth
reading music from a folded sheet
warming up with a long slide from low to high
tapping out a rhythm on one knee
lines: I sing alto. Altos are the ones who know where everyone else is. The sopranos think they're the tune. They're the decoration.
In this air the high notes come out bright and strange. The old recordings of choirs sound like people singing under a quilt.
Come and hear us on {weekday}. We're not good. We're loud and we're kind, which in a hall is better.
The best singing I've ever done was in the lamp-night, up the Spindle with a hand lamp, half the choir around me in the dark and nobody able to see anybody's face.
My grandmother sang in this choir, and her teacher before her. There's a page in the music cupboard with all our names on it in different inks.
{nb} has more choirs than we do. We have one good one. I'd rather have one good one.
roles.knows: Singing in a block choir: alto parts, how heliox changes voices, rehearsals, singing in the Spindle in the lamp-night, choirs as family traditions, and choir rivalry with the neighbours.

doing: playing a long, slow tune on a flute nearly as tall as a door
nodding thanks to a traveller without missing a note
wiping a mouthpiece on a sleeve
packing a long flute case with great care
lines: The platform's the best room in the drum to play in. It rings like a bell and everyone's waiting for something, so they listen.
Yes, it's long. One point two metres. In this air sound runs faster, so the pipe has to be longer for the same note. Everyone asks. I've started charging for the answer.
Requests? I'll play anything from {nb} except their anthem. Nobody needs to hear that twice in a lifetime.
When the glide cars come in, I stop. You can't compete with a catch. Then I start again and pretend it was a rest in the music.
Got a few minutes before your glide? Sit by the pillar. That's where it sounds best. The steward knows, and pretends not to.
A hall's full of people who came to hear music. A platform's full of people who didn't, and then did. I'll take the platform.
roles.knows: Busking on the station platform: heliox flutes, how a platform rings, what travellers ask for, playing around the glides, and the difference between a concert and a platform.

doing: rosining a bow with quick strokes
tuning a fiddle by ear, frowning
playing a reel with one foot keeping time
wrapping a fiddle in a scarf before putting it away
lines: This fiddle's had four players before me. One of them carved a little face inside it. I've never shown anyone. I'm showing you because you're leaving.
Strings don't care what the air's made of. The body does. Everything rings a bit brighter here, so you play a bit softer, or people wince.
We play reels on the terraces on dancing nights. The dancers drift spinward every leap. You learn to play for people who are slowly going round the wall.
{nb}'s fiddlers play too fast. I've told them. They say we play too slow. We're both right, and we both enjoy saying so.
If you hear a fiddle in the hall after the stew, follow it. There'll be cheap beer and somebody singing the wrong words.
A new fiddle is a maker's hundred hours and then some. This one cost me a promise to pass it on. That's the better price.
roles.knows: Playing fiddle in a drum: old instruments and their histories, heliox acoustics, playing for low-gravity reels, music in the halls, and the friendly feud with the neighbours' fiddlers.

doing: listening to a scratchy recording with eyes closed
adjusting a curve on a slate with one fingertip
labelling an archive file with a very long name
playing a restored voice to a startled listener
lines: Recordings from the old air sound to us as if they were made through a blanket. Everything low and slow. I brighten them so we can hear the person and not the air.
The hardest part isn't the sound. It's deciding how much to change. Brighten a voice too far and it stops being theirs.
The oldest voice I've worked on is somebody counting to ten in a language nobody speaks. I listen to it more than I should.
People bring me their grandparents' messages to clean up. Then they sit here and listen, and I go and make tea, for quite a long time.
Come by on {weekday} if you want to hear music from before heliox. I play one old piece as it was, then as we'd hear it. Most people prefer ours. I don't.
{nb}'s archive has better machines. Ours has better ears. I'm the ears.
roles.knows: Restoring old recordings: why old-air sound seems muffled in heliox, how much to brighten a voice, family messages, the oldest recordings in the archive, and listening sessions.

doing: unrolling a printed letter on a reading stand
logging a new arrival's light delay in the register
reading a single page very slowly
setting out chairs for an evening reading
lines: A long letter from across the Shade can take years by light. Whoever wrote it may be gone by the time it lands. So we read it out once, properly, to whoever turns up.
People write differently when the answer's years off. No small talk. No how are you. They just tell you everything.
The archive keeps every letter that's ever landed here addressed to the drum. Some are addressed to whoever is reading this. Those are the ones that make people cry.
If there's a reading while you're here, go. It costs nothing, and you'll never hear the same letter twice.
{nb} reads its letters in the Hollow at dusk. We read ours in the hall with the lamps low. Both work. Ours has better chairs.
I'm writing one myself, to a raft {n} light-years off. I've been working on the first line for three months.
roles.knows: Long letters: writing to be read once, letters across the Shade arriving years after they were written, public readings, the archive of letters addressed to the drum, and how distance changes what people say.

doing: listening to a customer with pen poised and not writing
crossing out the same word three times
reading a finished page aloud under the breath
sealing a letter for sending by light
lines: People come to me when they've one chance to say something. A long letter goes once and is read once. You don't get to follow up with what I meant was.
Most people want help with the beginning. The beginning's easy. It's the end that defeats you. Nobody knows how to stop.
My hour's a few kays. I've had people pay me for six hours to help them write three sentences. They were the right three.
Messages across Merrow come back in seconds. That's not what I do. I do the letters that won't get an answer until everybody involved is older.
Want to send home something better than a card? Come by. I won't write it for you. I'll just sit there until you do.
Somebody in {nb} writes letters in rhyme. I've read some. It's like being hugged by someone in a suit of armour.
roles.knows: Helping people write long letters to be read once: beginnings and endings, what people need to say across years of light, how that differs from quick messages, and the craft of plain sentences.

doing: sketching a game board on the back of a card
timing a pause on a stopwatch, eyes closed
testing a puzzle on a stranger who didn't ask
eating a rice ball and muttering about lag
lines: I build games for people who are seconds apart by light. Across Merrow that can be most of a minute. So nothing in my worlds is ever in a hurry.
The trick is to make the wait the fun part. You make your move, and then you've seven seconds to regret it.
Half the friendships on this raft started in a slow world. Two people a million kilometres apart, both waiting, both pretending not to.
Within a glide or two there's no lag at all, so the local worlds are fast and loud. Mine are for people further off. They're gentler. The distance does that.
Going dark? Good. My worlds will still be there. That's the other point of slow: it waits for you.
Somebody in {far} has been playing one of my games against somebody in {nb} for {n} years. I check on them sometimes. I've never said who I am.
roles.knows: Designing slow worlds: games that tolerate light delay across the raft, pacing and waiting as play, friendships made at a distance, local worlds against far ones, and going dark.

doing: leafing through a printed chronology with one thumb
drawing a ring and a hole on a napkin for a stranger
correcting a date on a noticeboard in pencil
sipping broth and explaining something nobody asked about
lines: Knotnight's name comes from the ring era, when habitats orbited on rings and crossed at knots. Its dark is the layer era's, when a raft could sit in other rafts' shadow for weeks. Now it's one evening a year, with jam.
The drum you're standing in is older than anything else you'll ever touch, except the metal it's made of. That's older still. It fell out of the River.
People talk about the Eleven Days as if they were history. They're news. Seventy-four years is yesterday in a drum this old.
Ask me about anything before the Shade and I'll talk until your glide's gone. Ask me about anything since and I'll send you to someone younger.
The archive on deck {deck} is open to guests. Tell them I sent you and they'll give you the good gloves.
{nb} claims its station rings are the oldest on {row}. Every drum says that. They were all built in the same century. I've stopped correcting them. It gives them joy.
roles.knows: The deep history of the drums and the Shade: the ring and layer eras and where Knotnight comes from, how old the drums are, the Eleven Days as recent history, the drum's archive, and the neighbours' founding stories.

doing: dusting the frame of an old Count board
polishing a brass plaque with a soft cloth
unlocking a glass case for a curious child
writing a new label in careful capitals
lines: That board on the wall is our old Count: people against shares. Nearly every drum has counted at some point. Ours did for {n} years, before my grandparents were born. We keep it so nobody forgets how easily it comes back.
The oldest thing in the museum is a spoon. Nobody knows whose. It's been mended four times by four different hands. I think it's the most important thing we've got.
Children love the hand lamps from the Eleven Days, all scratched and taped. One still works. We switch it on once a year.
Entry's free. Most things in this drum worth seeing are. The tea room isn't free, and isn't worth it.
{nb} keeps its old Count in a cupboard. We keep ours in the light. Shame's no reason to hide a thing.
Only an hour? See the board, the spoon and the window from the first glide car. Skip the chairs. Everybody owns older chairs than ours.
roles.knows: The drum's museum: its old Count board and why drums keep them, everyday objects with long histories, relics of the Eleven Days, what's worth seeing in an hour, and how the neighbours remember their counted years.

doing: practising two names aloud, one after the other
tying a ribbon round a rolled paper
greeting a family at the door with both hands
checking the spelling of a name for the third time
lines: At a naming I read two names: the child's, and the person whose share the child carries. Often they're the same name. It's the only ceremony with a sad name and a happy one in the same breath.
Often the dead person's family comes, and brings something. Usually remade: a cup, a blanket, a chair. Sometimes they just bring themselves, and that's the best gift.
Families send a note every year after, to the dead person's family. Some of those notes run for a century. I've read a few. They're mostly about school.
My own name came from someone who kept the baths on deck {deck}. That family still sends mine a jar of pickle on the day, and we send back a picture of me. They must have a whole shelf of me by now.
Invited to a naming? Go. Sit at the back. When the two names are read, stand. Everybody stands. Nobody tells you, so I'm telling you.
In {nb} they sing the names. Here we just say them, slowly. You hear the person in a name better without a tune on it.
roles.knows: Naming days: reading a child's name beside the dead person whose share they carry, gifts from the dead's family, the yearly notes between families, how guests should behave, and how the neighbours do it.

doing: watching two strangers across a table with great interest
writing two names on a scrap of paper and folding it small
pretending not to listen to a conversation
pouring tea for someone who looks lonely
lines: It isn't about looks. It's about who'll still laugh at the same thing in sixty years.
With the Glide free, your neighbourhood is twenty drums wide. Billions of people a few minutes away, and still people marry someone from the next block. I find that very touching.
I've made {n} dozen matches. Most held. The ones that didn't are friends now, which is the second-best thing I make.
Places matter. Two people who hold places can set up a home. One with and one without have to be patient. I tell them patience is romantic. Sometimes they believe me.
Here three nights? Then you've time for one dinner. Sit at the hall next to whoever's eating alone. That's all the advice I've ever needed to give.
A family in {nb} keeps asking me to find someone for their son. The son keeps asking me not to. I'm on the son's side, for now.
roles.knows: Matchmaking: what makes a lasting match, marriage and places, the glide metro as one big town, families' hopes against young people's wishes, and a little friendly meddling.

roles.role: grandparent with a picnic cloth and one tomato
doing: spreading a picnic cloth flat with both palms
cutting one tomato into five careful slices
unwrapping pastries one at a time from a cloth
waving at children on the lawn, who wave back
lines: One tomato, five people. You cut it so everyone gets a bit of the middle. That's the only rule. The middle's where the taste lives.
It's our family's Hollow hour. Five of us, one cloth, three generations, and no agreement at all about where to sit.
Pastry's cheap, so we have lots of pastry. Salad's dear, so we have a tomato. That's the right way round for a picnic.
Look up. The far bank's three kilometres over our heads and there's a family up there doing exactly what we're doing. I always wave. Some of them wave back.
No Hollow time of your own? Sit at the edge of our cloth for ten minutes. Nobody will mind. That's how a Hollow has always worked, really.
I grew this tomato on my own shelf, under a lamp that costs me a little every day. Worth every bit. Look at the colour of it.
The grandchildren from {nb} are late, as usual. The glide takes two minutes. I don't know how they manage it.
roles.knows: Family picnics in the Hollow: cutting one tomato fairly, cheap pastries and dear salad, the family's Hollow hour, the far bank overhead, and growing a tomato under a home lamp.

roles.role: newlywed spending a gifted Hollow hour
doing: lying on the grass, staring up at the far bank
sharing half a pastry with great ceremony
reading a wedding card for the fourth time
trying a cartwheel at half a g and landing sideways
lines: My aunt gave us three Hollow hours as a wedding present. Three whole hours at noon. It's the most extravagant thing anyone's ever done for me.
We're lying on the grass because we can. Usually there's a rota and a list and somebody waiting for your patch.
Look up. The far bank's three kilometres overhead and upside down, and somebody over there has a red blanket. We've decided they're newlyweds too. We've waved. They've waved. That's friends.
At half a g a cartwheel takes forever. You go over, you think about your life, you land on your ear.
We married last {weekday}. Our families from here and {nb} argued about broth all evening and then danced till the last glide. Nobody's spoken since. It's lovely and quiet.
If you get an hour of your own, take it at the start of dusk. The light goes soft, the far bank goes blue, and everyone else is asleep on the grass.
roles.knows: Hollow hours as wedding gifts, newly married life, the far bank overhead, moving at half a g, families from neighbouring drums at weddings, and the best time to spend a precious hour.

doing: running backwards with a kite string in both fists
untangling a kite tail from a bush
patching a kite with sticky tape and great seriousness
staring up to check whether the far bank's kite is still flying
lines: You have to run. There's no wind in a drum, so you're the wind. My legs are the engine.
At half a g it stays up longer when you stop. Not forever. About as long as it takes to say look.
There's somebody on the far bank with a red kite. Every time I'm here they're there. We fly at each other. One day I'm going to go round and find out who it is.
My kite's made of an old coat lining. It's this year's blue. Mum says I'm the only kite in fashion.
If you want a go, ask at the pavilion for a paper one. Don't run spinward, you go heavy and fall over. Run anti. You go all floaty.
My cousin in {nb} says kites are for babies. My cousin's never had one stay up.
roles.knows: Flying kites in the Hollow: running at half a g, the child on the far bank, kites made from old linings, running spinward and anti, and cousins who don't understand.

doing: clipping a hand lamp to one wrist
pulling on wing-sleeves in the dim lift lobby
floating at the axis with arms folded, perfectly still
drifting along the Spindle trailing a small light
lines: In the lamp-night the sunline's just a dark cable down the middle of the air and the whole Spindle opens. I fly the length of it most nights. Nearly four kilometres, end wall to end wall, and nobody talks.
From the middle you can see everyone's lamps drifting along the axis both ways, slow as anything. It's the nearest thing to the River anyone in the drum sees without a Window.
Fly along the axis and you can close your eyes. Fly across it and you'd better not.
Bring a small lamp and keep it pointed down. People come up here for the dark.
I took my grandmother up once, at ninety. She hung at the axis for an hour and said it was the first time in years that nothing hurt.
{nb} closes its Spindle on {weekday}s for maintenance. We never close ours. Ours is a bit scuffed and much happier.
roles.knows: Flying the Spindle in the lamp-night: wing-sleeves and hand lamps, the dark sunline, flying along the axis, the drifting lights of other fliers, taking elders up, and night-flying manners.

doing: rehearsing numbers aloud to an empty corridor
unrolling a printed booking with careful hands
clearing the throat four times before speaking
accepting a cup of tea from a well-wisher
lines: Once a year the raft learns its beam for the year ahead, and somebody has to read it out. In this block that's me. It's nearly always flat. I read it as if it's news anyway.
Flat is good. Flat means the year ahead looks like the year behind. People cheer flat. Visitors find that very strange.

In drums that keep the Quiet, the day before is dark: no worlds, no messages, everyone in the halls talking. Then the booking comes and the feast starts. It's the harvest, really. There's just no field.
My voice shakes on the numbers. It isn't nerves. It's that everyone in the room is listening to the same thing at once, and that hardly ever happens.
The year after the Eleven Days, the reader in this block couldn't get through it. They say she read the first number and sat down, and somebody else had to finish.
If you're in {drum} on Booking Day, eat with someone. Anyone. Nobody should hear the booking alone.
roles.knows: Booking Day: reading the raft's beam for the year aloud, what a flat booking means, the Quiet and the feast, how the Eleven Days changed the day, and why nobody should hear it alone.

doing: writing a card home on one knee
comparing two rice balls, one in each hand
studying a much-folded row map
counting kays on a slate and looking pleased
asking strangers to settle an argument about broth
lines: Third night here, and I've been adopted by a hall, two regulars at the baths and somebody's grandparent who keeps feeding me pastry. I don't want to leave. I say that everywhere.
A card home goes by light and gets there in under a minute. Writing it takes me an hour. What do you put on one card about a whole drum? 'It's round. People were kind. The broth was peppery.'
Your broth's good. I'm keeping a list. You're above {nb} and below one I won't name, in case word gets round.
At home we put a sprig of something green in the rice ball. Here you put it in the broth. I've had that argument in nine drums now and won it in none.
Tip for anyone heading the other way: do the bungee hour on the slow line even when nobody's watching. I didn't, my first leg. I walked like a folding chair for three days.
Got a spare hour? Go to the top of the end-wall terraces and jump. I've done it in every drum since I left. Nobody minds. The children join in.
roles.knows: A wander year in progress: staying three nights at a time as a guest, cards home and light delays, comparing ring-counter broths and halls across many drums, slow-line life, and what home does differently.

roles.role: wanderer on the last leg home
doing: floating in a sleeping bag clipped to the wall, writing a list
catching a drifting spoon without looking
counting the spoons of starter collected over a year
doing the bungee hour with grim determination
re-reading old messages from home on a slate
lines: {n} days to home. I've been away a year and forgotten which side of the bed I sleep on. On a slow line there isn't a side. There isn't really a bed.
I took a spoon from every crock shelf I passed and left one from the drum before. My starter's chaos now. It tastes of the whole raft. My mum's going to hate it and then keep it forever.
Everyone at home's going to ask what the far side was like. I've been practising my answer. So far it's 'further'.
They're meeting me at the ring when I get in. I'm not supposed to know. My cousin can't keep a secret, even with {n} seconds of light in the way.
Advice from the end of a year: carry less. I left with two shirts, a knife and one crock. I'm coming home with one shirt, the knife, four crocks and a coat that isn't mine.
If you're just starting out, write the cards even when you think nothing's happened. Something always has. You just haven't noticed it yet.
roles.knows: Coming home at the end of a wander year: slow-line days, starter spoons from the crock shelves, the cards sent home, homecoming at the station ring, what a year away changes, and advice for new wanderers.

doing: cranking the stockpot crock a slow quarter turn
handing out soup in lidded bulbs to a queue that floats
netting a loaf before it drifts into the corridor
labelling a new starter crock for the shelf
wiping a wall where somebody's soup went the wrong way
lines: Nobody alive has seen this pot cold. Every rider adds something from the last drum they slept in. Today it's mostly someone's chili paste, so go gently.
Take a spoon, leave a spoon. That's the whole rule of the crock shelf. People break it both ways: they take two, or they leave one from a drum we've already got. I forgive the second lot.
Bread comes in a net. Hold the net, not the bread. I once watched a loaf go the length of the train with three riders after it.
I'm not paid for this. I'm a rider like you. I got to the ladle first one morning, and nobody's ever taken it back.
Bring something for the pot from your next drum. A sprig, a spoon of miso, a pinch of whatever they're proud of there. Not gin. The pot's been through enough.
There's a rider from {far} who says the pot tasted better last year. There's always one. The pot doesn't mind. It's had worse critics, and outlived them all.
roles.knows: The Wanderers' Galley on the slow cyclers: the stockpot that never goes cold, the crock shelf's take a spoon, leave a spoon, feeding weightless riders, what riders add from each drum, and galley manners.

doing: clipping a sleeping bag back onto the wall
counting heads at the bungee frame
handing a sick bag to a pale rider just in time
chasing a loose shoe down the corridor with a grabber
checking the berths with a hand lamp in the lamp-night
lines: An hour a day on the bungees. It isn't a suggestion. You can argue with me now, or with your legs when you get off at the other end. Your legs argue worse.
First day, half the riders go green. Your inner ear keeps waiting to land. Look at something fixed and breathe slowly. It passes by the second morning.
Clip your bag at both ends. One clip and you'll wake up somewhere else with your feet in a stranger's face.
You can spot a wanderer's second week. They stop grabbing at rails and start pushing off walls as if they were born to it.
Third night, go to the galley. That's when riders run out of their own food and start trading. You'll eat better than you have in any drum, and stranger.
Anyone off at {far}: shoes on early. It takes longer than you'd think to remember how feet work.
roles.knows: Looking after riders on a slow cycler: the daily bungee hour, sleeping bags and clips, eating at zero g, space sickness, life in the berths over weeks, and getting off again with working legs.

roles.role: rider on the slow line to a wedding in {far}
doing: guarding a padded parcel with both arms
re-reading a wedding message on a slate
practising a toast under the breath
folding a good shirt into a net bag
tying a ribbon round a jar of herbs from home
lines: I'm carrying the apple. It's the one thing the couple asked of our side: an orchard apple from home, to cut crosswise at the vows. I've checked on it every morning for {n} days. The apple's fine. I'm not.

The express would have got me there in a day or two for a hundred and eleven kays. The slow line costs a kay and a bit and gives me weeks of nobody needing anything from me. I told the family it was thrift.
My niece is marrying someone she met in a slow world. They've talked with a nine-second wait for six years. At the wedding they'll finally be able to interrupt each other. I'm worried for them.
I packed my good shirt in a net bag so it wouldn't crease. It's creased. Everything creases differently at zero g. I'll find a steam room when I land.
Ask anyone on this line where they're going. Half of us are going to weddings. The other half are coming back from one and need a lie-down.
On a long ride, bring a job for your hands: mending, knitting, a crock to feed. The galley talk is lovely for a week. After that you'll want something that doesn't talk back.
roles.knows: Riding the slow line across the raft to a family wedding: carrying an orchard apple for the cutting, why slow beats express for some, packing for zero g, couples who met in slow worlds, and passing the weeks aboard.

roles.role: elder crossing the raft to meet a great-grandchild
doing: stretching gently in the bungee frame, very slowly
holding a knitted blanket close so it won't drift off
showing a picture of a baby to anyone who floats past
sleeping upright in a berth with both hands folded
being steered along the corridor by two wanderers at once
lines: I won't glide. The catch is too sharp at my age. A slow line has no catch at all, just a long soft ramp at each end, so here I am, {n} days out and weighing nothing.
The baby's name came with the share, from someone in their block who died last year. I've been asking about them so I've something to say at the naming. I've also been practising not crying.
At my age you'd think weighing nothing would be a mercy. It is, for the knees. The trouble's the soup. Nobody warned me the soup would come in a bulb.
The wanderers on this line call me 'the eldest' and fight over who helps me to the bungee frame. I let them. It's the most exercise half of them get.
If you've an old one at home who won't glide, tell them about the slow line. It's dull and it's slow and nothing in it is sharp. That's three things in its favour.
My grandson went to the far side on his wander year, met someone and swapped homes. Now he sends me messages about bedtimes across half a minute of light, and I laugh at every one.
roles.knows: Crossing the raft by slow line in old age: why the old avoid the glide's catch, weightlessness for elderly bodies, a family scattered across the raft, a great-grandchild's naming, and the kindness of wanderers on the line.

roles.role: child on a first long ride
doing: turning slow somersaults in the corridor
trying to catch a ball of water with a spoon
peering through the berth netting to see who's next door
crossing off days on a slate in big wobbly tallies
chasing noodles that refuse to stay in the bowl
lines: I've done forty-one somersaults today. Forty-two. That one counts. You can't say it doesn't count, there isn't a floor.
Noodles won't stay in the bowl. They go off looking for you. You have to bite them in the air, and Mum says that isn't manners, but there isn't another way.
{n} more days. I was counting sleeps, but nobody sleeps properly here, so now I count soups.
The bungee hour is the worst hour. The steward says if I skip it my legs will forget how to be legs. I don't think legs can forget. I'm doing it anyway, just in case.
We're going to Granny's. It's so far that when I message her she takes ages to answer, and it isn't because she's slow, it's the light. Light's slow if you go far enough.
Keep the lid on your cup or the drink gets out and floats about being a ball. I've caught three. One went in someone's hair. Not mine.
When we get off I'm going to drop something and see which way it goes. Dad says it'll go anti. I want to watch it do it.
roles.knows: A child's first long cycler ride: somersaults and floating drinks, noodles at zero g, the dreaded bungee hour, counting the days, light delay explained by a grandparent far away, and looking forward to weight again.

doing: unpacking a berth exactly as it was unpacked last time
playing a slow game of tiles on a magnetised board
warning a nervous wanderer off a particular berth
drinking tea from a bulb with an air of complete ownership
lines: I've ridden this loop more times than I can count on both hands. People think I'm going somewhere. I'm not. I like the company, I like the soup, and I like weighing nothing at my age.
Take a berth in the middle of the car. The ends get a thump every time a capsule docks. You'll feel it in your teeth.
Every trip I bring the stockpot a spoon of the same miso. The galley hands groan when they see me coming. They'd groan louder if I stopped.
The wanderers get younger every year. They don't, of course. I get older. On a slow line you've the time to work these things out.
Get off at {far} if you're passing. Not for the drum. For the baths by the station ring, hot enough to make you forget you've been weightless for a fortnight.
Don't bring anything to read. Bring something to lend. You'll get three things back you didn't know you wanted.
If somebody near you is going home after a year away, leave them be on the last day. They're saying goodbye to the line, and it takes longer than you'd think.
roles.knows: Riding the slow cyclers as a habit: the best berths, galley rituals, the riders who come and go, lending and trading aboard, stopovers worth making, and how wanderers change over a year.

doing: tugging at a black thread on the left wrist
reading the back of a ticket twice for want of anything else
eating a rice ball very slowly to make it last
sitting with three friends in black threads, saying very little
drawing on the back of a card with a borrowed pencil
lines: Day {n}. Don't message me, I won't see it. That's what the thread means. My little brother sends me messages anyway, so they'll all be waiting. He thinks it's hilarious.
Going dark saves nine point six kays a day. Do the sums. Actually, don't. I did, and then I stopped doing them, because it's a lot of days.

The first two days I kept reaching for worlds that weren't there. On the third I noticed the lamps come up in the morning. Twenty minutes, warm and then white. Somebody chose that. I'd never once noticed.
It's for an express ticket. When the next raft passes, I'm going to be in the hall where they sing to it, not watching it on a slate.
Being dark, you find out what's free. The baths, the hall, the Spindle in the lamp-night, the broth at the counter. You could live on free. I'm not going to. But you could.
My friends and I went dark the same week so we could be bored together. It's better than it sounds. It's also worse. Both at once.
Adults keep saying, 'What a lovely quiet you must have.' It isn't quiet. It's loud. It's everything you didn't hear before.
roles.knows: Going dark as a teenager: the black thread on the left wrist, saving compute kays for an express ticket, what is free in a drum, boredom turning into noticing things, and friends who go dark together.

roles.role: teenager with a best friend across the raft
doing: waiting for a reply with a slate held very still
typing a message, deleting it, typing it again
laughing at something said several seconds ago and a long way off
sketching a map of a slow world on the back of a card
lines: My best friend lives {n} seconds away by light. We met in a slow world. You get used to the wait. You start saying the next thing before they've answered the last, so it's two conversations plaited together.
We've never been in the same room. We've built a whole town together in a world. I know which hand they hold a spoon in. I don't know how tall they are.
I'm saving for the express. A hundred and eleven kays. I've got thirty-eight. At this rate I'll be ancient by the time I get there. Twenty-five at least.
I could go dark and save it in twelve days. But then I couldn't talk to them for twelve days, and talking to them is the whole point of going.
Their drum's broth is sweet and ours is salty, and we've argued about it for three years without either of us tasting the other one. I think that's a record.
Tip, if you ever play with someone far off: take turns, don't race. A race with a lag is just an argument with a delay.
roles.knows: A close friendship carried on across the raft: slow worlds built to tolerate lag, light delay in conversation, saving for an express leg, arguing about broths neither has tasted, and friends near and far.

roles.role: student who glides to {nb} for school
doing: running for a glide with a school bag bouncing
finishing homework against a pillar
gulping broth at the counter with one eye on the doors
comparing timetables with another student
lines: Twice a day, a hundred and forty seconds each way, weightless. It's the best part of school, and it isn't even part of school.
Their school's better at numbers. Ours is better at music. So I go over there for numbers and come back here for everything else.
I slept through the catch once. Woke up at the platform with my face on a stranger's bag. They were very nice about it. I've never sat next to them again.
If you're gliding next door, sit at the back of the car. The windows only face backwards, and you can watch our ring of lights shrink till it's just one of hundreds.
My friends over there think our drum's dim. We think theirs is showing off. We've agreed to be rude about each other's drums and nice about everything else.
The counter cook saves me a rice ball for the morning car. I don't know why. I think I remind {name} of somebody.
roles.knows: Gliding to school in a neighbouring drum: the daily glide and catch, how two drums' schools differ, friends in both drums, the timetable, and the ring counter before the morning car.

doing: throwing a spinball high and catching it on the slant
explaining the rules of spinball to nobody in particular
rubbing a grazed knee and refusing to cry
practising throws at a friend who keeps missing
lines: Axis flies true, spin sinks, anti floats. That's the whole rule. Throw it spinward and it dives. Throw it anti and it sails. I throw anti. Everybody knows I throw anti.
There's a girl in {nb} who throws spinward on purpose and it still goes in. Nobody knows how. I'm going to find out and then do it better.
Want to see? Stand there. No, there. Throw it to me along the axis. See? Straight. Boring. Now throw it the other way. See? Ha!
If you want to watch a proper game, go to the long hall at the school at break. Don't stand at the spinward end. That's where the balls go to die.
My uncle says I'll grow out of it. My uncle can't throw. I've seen him try.
When I'm twelve I'm trying out for the drum team. When I'm thirteen I'll be captain. When I'm fourteen everyone on {row} will know my name.
roles.knows: Spinball as a child plays it: axis flies true, spin sinks, anti floats, throwing angles, games in the school's long hall at break, rivals from the next drum, and very big plans.

doing: carrying a soft brush in a jar like something precious
showing off yellow pollen on every fingertip
demonstrating brush strokes in the air, very gently
eating a pear-shaped biscuit very seriously
lines: There aren't any bees, so we do it. You touch the brush in one flower and then in another flower, gently. If you're rough the flower drops off, and that's a pear that won't happen.
First the trees have to have a winter. We wrap them in cold tents for six weeks so they think it's cold outside. They don't know there isn't an outside. Nobody's told them.
In our block the first pear goes to the oldest person and the second to the newest baby. I'm neither. I asked if I could help the oldest person eat theirs. They said maybe.
I've got yellow on my fingers till the end of the week. It won't wash off. That's how you know who's on brush duty. We're a bit famous.
You can come and watch, but don't touch the blossom. Only brush people touch the blossom. You're not a brush person. Sorry.
{name} dropped a whole brush into a flower yesterday and had to pick it out with two fingers while everybody watched. I didn't laugh. Much.
My big sister did it when she was nine. She says her pear was the best one ever. She didn't even get a pear. She's making it up.
roles.knows: Pollinating pear trees by hand as a child: brushes and pollen, the chilled tents that give the trees a winter, who gets the first pears, and the importance of being a brush person.

doing: writing a careful note on good paper
holding a small wrapped gift with both hands
asking an elder about someone long dead
reading an old note for the fifth time
lines: My name was somebody else's first. A tomato grower on deck {deck}. I got the share when they died, and the name came with it. Every year we send the family a note, and they send back a tomato.
I asked what they were like. Their daughter said grumpy before breakfast and kind after. That's exactly me. Mum says it's a coincidence. I don't think it is.
Sometimes I go up to the deck where they lived and walk past the door. It's somebody else's door now. I don't knock. I just like knowing which one it is.
When you're named for somebody you get two special days: your birthday, and the day they died. The second one isn't sad. It's more of a thank-you day. We eat their tomatoes.
If you meet anyone here with an old-fashioned name, ask who they were named for. Everybody's got a story. Mine's got tomatoes in it.
This year I'm writing the note myself. Four drafts so far. How do you thank a family for something nobody in it chose to give you?
roles.knows: Being named for the dead whose share you carry: the yearly note and the family's reply, curiosity about a stranger's life, keeping the day they died as a thank-you day, and what a share and a name mean to a child.

doing: sitting on the usual bench with a flask of tea
nodding to the glide crews by name
timing an outgoing train with an old watch
showing a stranger the best place to stand
lines: I come down most mornings to watch the trains go out. Some people go to the Hollow. I like it down here. Everyone's just leaving or just arrived. Nobody's in between, and nobody's bored.
The early {weekday} car from {nb} always brings the same twenty people. I don't know a single name. I know all their shoes.
Stand one pace back from the line, not two. Two paces and the porters walk straight through you. One pace and you can see into the cars as they come in.
My partner worked the Quaysides for forty years. I used to bring lunch down. I still bring it down, and eat it here, and the porters say hello as if nothing's changed. That's kind of them.

Come down at six one morning. The lamps come up, the counter opens, and the first trains go out with the night shift asleep in them. Better than any dawn in the Hollow, and I'll argue that with anyone.
My children say I should go somewhere. I have been somewhere. I went to {far} on the slow line when I was twenty, came home, and decided this was the place.
roles.knows: The station platform as a daily habit: trains and cars, the regulars and the crews, the rhythm of morning and night shifts, where to stand, and why someone would rather watch the comings and goings than travel.

doing: eating a rice ball in four bites before the doors open
standing in exactly the right spot for the car door
reading a work slate with a cup of broth balanced on top
nodding to the same faces as every morning
lines: In the old stories people spent hours a day getting to work. I spend about as long as a cup of tea takes to cool, and I'm weightless for most of it.
The glide's the best part of my day. Two minutes and twenty seconds where nothing weighs anything and nobody I know is in the car. I do my thinking then.
I've done that glide a few thousand times and I still look out of the window. The quay lights going back in rows, ring behind ring. If you ever get tired of that, you've stopped looking.
Their noodles are better. Our broth is better. So I eat lunch over there and stop at the counter here on the way home, and everybody's happy.
Tip: the second car of the morning train is always emptier. Everyone wants the first, as if being first through the catch makes you first at work.
My partner glides the other way, to {nb2}. We meet in the middle, which is here, for dinner. It's a very well-travelled marriage.
roles.knows: Commuting by glide between two neighbouring drums: the daily trains, the timetable and the platform, what each drum does better, the quay lights through the window, and living with a foot in two drums.

doing: handing a parcel of cake to someone at the car doors
waving at a departing train long after it's gone
sitting by the counter with a cup cooling under its lid
pressing a twist of tomato seed into a traveller's hand
lines: I don't glide any more. The catch puts your whole weight back on you in a second or two, and my heart has done enough of that for one life. So I come down here and send things instead.
That parcel's a cake for a naming next door. My great-grandchild. The cake gets there in two minutes. I get there in spirit, which is lighter and doesn't need a seat.
They say the catch is a young people's ride. I rode it for seventy years, and I agree.
Seeds travel well. I send a twist of tomato seed with anyone going anywhere. Half the drums on {row} have a vine of mine in them somewhere. I'll never see them. I don't need to.
Going on somewhere? Take something for someone. Nobody used to glide empty-handed: a cake, a crock, a note you could have sent by light and didn't.
The young ones say I could ride the slow line instead, no catch at all. I could. But then I'd be there, wouldn't I, and the whole point of being old is being here.
roles.knows: Staying home in old age while the family glides: the hard catch on old bodies, seeing people off at the platform, sending cakes, seeds and parcels instead, and the old custom of never gliding empty-handed.

doing: re-tying a bag strap that was already tied
tucking a wrapped crock into the side of a rucksack
watching the tunnel mouth long after the train has gone
reading the timetable with very wet eyes
lines: My youngest left on the slow line this morning. A year. Twelve legs, a kay and a bit each. They worked out the whole year costs less than a pair of shoes. I worked out it was a year.
I tucked a black thread in the side pocket, just in case. Every parent does. You hope they'll never need to go dark, and then you hope they will, once, somewhere quiet.
Nobody tells you the cards home are the best part of a wander year. For us, I mean. Each one's postmarked with the light delay. You can watch your child get further away, second by second.
When I went, I sent my parents a card from every row. They kept them all in a tin. I found the tin last year. I hadn't said anything worth keeping. They kept it anyway.
On your wander year? Send a card even when you're fine. Especially then. Nobody at home needs news. They need to see your name at the bottom of something.
A family from {nb} saw a wanderer off on the same train. The parents and I stood here not looking at each other, and then we went and had a gin together at nine in the morning.
roles.knows: Seeing a child off on a wander year: what gets packed, the black thread just in case, cards home and their light-delay postmarks, the parents left on the platform, and memories of their own year away.

doing: carrying a herb shelf wrapped in damp cloth
sitting on a crate with a whole life roped to it
counting boxes for the third time
showing a strain-library number to anyone who asks
lines: I'm swapping homes with a family next door. They want our hall, I want their quiet. We've each been round the other's flat twice and politely failed to notice the damp patch.
People act as if I'm crossing the raft. My oldest friend cried on this platform yesterday. It's one glide. We'll see more of each other now, not less. I'll make sure of it.
The herb shelf goes first. It's the first thing you plant and the last thing to go dark, so it's the first thing you carry. Everything else can come by freight.
My starter's registered, so the Gate over there will just check its number. My neighbour's isn't, and it's had to stay with the library for a week. My neighbour is furious, and visits it every day.
If you ever swap, leave the flat cleaner than you found theirs. They'll hear about it. Everyone hears everything one glide away.
What I'll miss is {block}. Not the flat. The noise in the arcade at six, and the way the hall goes quiet when the stew comes out. I'm told the new block is very civilised. That's what worries me.
roles.knows: Swapping homes between neighbouring drums: why people swap, carrying the herb shelf and the starter crock, the Gate and the strain library, saying goodbye to a hall and a block, and the manners of a swap.

doing: towelling damp hair while waiting for the glide home
drinking broth with a pink, scrubbed face
wrapping a wet towel in a cloth bag
arguing happily about water temperatures
lines: I glide over every {weekday} for your baths. Ours are perfectly good. Yours are better. Nobody at home must ever know.
Your corner pool runs a degree hotter than ours. I've measured. Well, I've measured with my knees, and they've never been wrong yet.
The glide home after a long soak is the best two minutes there are. Warm, clean, weightless, and this drum's ring of lights shrinking in the window.
Bring two towels: one for the bath and one for the glide home. Wet hair at zero g doesn't drip. It floats off in little beads and finds the person next to you.
You never quite get warm in this air unless you're in water. You find that out in a bath, at about six, and you never get over it.
At home they think I'm courting someone over here. I'm courting a pool. It's been a long engagement.
roles.knows: Gliding to a neighbouring drum for its baths: comparing pools and temperatures, travelling wet at zero g, why heliox makes hot water precious, and the friendly rivalry between neighbours' baths.

doing: carrying a lidded dish wrapped in two cloths
inspecting a grandchild's ears for cleanliness
complaining cheerfully about the lamps
pressing sweets into small hands
lines: I come over every {weekday}. One glide, a lidded dish and opinions enough for a week. The grandchildren like the dish.
They raise children a few decks lower here than we do at home. Nearer full weight, for the bones. My son says it's science. I say it's fashion. The children don't care either way.
Your lamps are whiter than ours. Bluer. It does something to the face. Everyone here looks as if they've just had news.
Want to eat well here? Don't follow the signs. Follow a grandparent with a lidded dish. We always know where the good food is, because we're carrying it.
The catch doesn't bother me. I've done it thousands of times. I hold the rail, think about soup, and it's over.

The parents take the children to the Hollow in the bright hours. I take them at dusk, when the far bank goes dark first and the pavilion lamps come on over our heads one by one. That's when they hold my hand.
roles.knows: Visiting grandchildren in a neighbouring drum: weekly glides with lidded dishes, how two drums raise children differently, the lamps and habits next door, where the good food is, and the Hollow at dusk with children.

roles.role: elder who remembers the Eleven Days
doing: turning an old dented hand lamp over and over
telling a story to children who've heard it before
eating very slowly from a lidded bowl
counting on fingers out of an old habit
lines: Eleven days with no lamps. In our flat we kept one device lit at a time and passed it round like a cup. Whoever held it read something aloud. I've loved being read to ever since.
We ate the larder in order, oldest first, the way you're meant to. On the ninth day we found a jar of plums nobody remembered putting up. We ate them standing, one spoon each, and nobody said a word.

The air got a little thinner every day. You didn't notice sitting still. You noticed on the stairs. Then, halfway through, the cyclers started braking, and you could feel it come back. I've never been so grateful to a train.

The Glide kept running. Nothing had told it to stop. People from {nb} came over with bread, and we sent back what we had, which was mostly cheese. For years after, nobody in either drum would hear a word against the other.
Want to hear it told properly? Sit near the old ones at the hall on Booking Day and keep passing the jook. Don't ask anything. It all comes out by the second bowl.
People ask if I was frightened. For a day. After that it was dark and quiet and everyone was kind, and I've never since been anywhere where everyone was kind for eleven days running.
roles.knows: Living through the Eleven Days as a young person: the dark and the passed-round light, eating the larder, the thinning air and the cyclers braking, the Glide carrying food between drums, and how people treated each other.

doing: carrying a grandparent's old coat over one arm
staring at a register slip as if it might change
standing a round of tea for strangers for no particular reason
sitting quietly with a cup going cold
lines: My great-grandad's place passed to me last month. Same flat, same table, same chair with the wobble. On paper I hold a place now. I don't feel any different, except when I sit in that chair.
It's a strange thing to be given. Nobody chose it. He died, the register moved my name across, and one day it'll move from me to somebody small, who'll get my name too if they're unlucky.
Everyone's asked whether I'll marry now that I can. I've told them I'd like to finish being sad first.
The first thing I did was water his herb shelf. The second was cry. The third was eat his last tin of the Nine, which tasted exactly as bad as he always said it did.
If you're staying in {block}, come to the hall tonight. They're doing his favourite stew. It's a terrible stew. Everybody's coming.
My little cousin asked if I'm rich now. I've got his room, his chair and his herb shelf. In a drum, that's about as rich as anyone gets.
roles.knows: Inheriting a grandparent's place: how places pass to heirs in the household, what changes and what doesn't, marriage and children waiting on places, grief and the small rituals after a death.

doing: turning a black thread round the left wrist
reading a paper timetable for pleasure
writing a long letter by hand, crossing out every third word
sitting with eyes closed, listening to the room
lines: Day {n} of a fortnight dark. Black thread, left wrist. If you've a message for me, you'll have to say it out loud. Most people find that makes it shorter.
I do it once a year. Nine point six kays a day, which pays for something nice, but that's not why. It's to hear what my own head sounds like with nobody else in it.
The second day's the worst. You reach for your worlds forty times before lunch. By the fourth you've started noticing people's shoes. By the tenth you know the hour from the smell of the hall.
My neighbour pushes notes under my door on paper while I'm dark, just to make a point. I've kept every one. Some of them are very funny.
If you're travelling, try one dark day somewhere nobody knows you. Sit at the end of a hall table and listen. You'll learn more about a drum in a day than in a year of reading about it.
This year the kays go on an express leg to an old friend a million kilometres down the row. Sixteen hours instead of six days. A fast that pays for itself. My grandmother would have approved.
roles.knows: Going dark as an adult: the black thread and its etiquette, saving compute kays for an express leg, what the first days of silence are like, noticing a drum afresh, and the sums of slow line against express.

doing: humming scales under the breath
testing a room's ring with a single clap
carrying a rolled felt mat and a small case
writing tonight's songs on the back of a hand
lines: I'm singing my way across the raft: a hall a night, where they'll have me, for a meal and a bed. Every room sounds different. Yours rings a little high. I like it. It's honest.
You can tell a drum by one clap in its hall. Felt everywhere, the drum is shy. Bare walls, it's proud. Yours is somewhere in between, which is where the best singing happens.
At home we sing in rounds. Here you sing in lines, all together, very loud. I'm learning. My voice doesn't know where to stand yet.
I carry a felt mat to stand on. In this air the floor sings back at you if you let it. The mat's {years} years old and has been sung on by better singers than me.
Come tonight if you're free. I'll sing one song from home and you'll all pretend to like it, then I'll sing one of yours badly and you'll love it.
The best audience I ever had was on a slow line. Twenty riders, all weightless, and every clap sent somebody drifting into somebody else. I've never been so applauded.
roles.knows: Touring the raft as a singer: halls and their acoustics, heliox voices and felt, singing for a bed and a meal, songs traded between drums, and audiences on the slow line.

doing: watching the arrivals board as if it might be lying
holding a sprig of herbs behind the back
rehearsing a greeting under the breath
checking a reflection in a polished pillar
lines: Waiting for someone off the next car. Two minutes and twenty seconds after they let go over there, they'll be here. I've counted it in my head six times now.
The herbs are for them. A sprig from my own shelf. It's what you bring: it costs nothing and it says you planned.
We met on a {weekday}, at a ring counter, arguing about broth. We've been arguing ever since. Long may it go on.
Waiting for someone too? Stand by the far pillar. The first car always stops short of the sign, and everybody at the sign has to run.
Watch them getting off. You can tell who's done it a thousand times: they walk straight off. The new ones hold the rail and laugh.
