The car's late. No, it isn't. The Glide's never late, it can't be, it's falling. It's me. I came {n} minutes early.
roles.knows: Waiting on the platform for someone arriving by glide: the timing of arrivals, greeting customs and bringing herbs, how arrivals carry themselves, where to stand, and the nerves of meeting someone dear.

roles.role: great-grandparent in a coat with four owners' mends
doing: smoothing a mended sleeve with the flat of a hand
telling a great-grandchild to sit up straight
eating a pastry with great dignity and some crumbs
pointing out each patch on an old coat like stops on a map
lines: This coat's been worn by four of us, counting me. The elbows are my mother's work, the collar's her father's, and nobody remembers who did the pocket. Whoever asks nicely gets it next.
Every mend shows. I like it that way. A coat with no repairs is a coat nobody loved enough to fix.
I wore this through the Eleven Days. Slept in it, mostly. It smelled of the larder for a year afterwards, cheese and miso. I miss that smell.
I've got {n} great-grandchildren and every one of them wants the coat. I've promised it to each of them. I'll be gone before they compare notes.
If you want something warm here, don't buy new. Ask a mender what's been left behind. Half the coats on {street} are older than me, and I'm older than most things.
Young people wear their coats done up. We wore them open, so the lining showed. That's what a lining's for.
roles.knows: A long life in a thrifty drum: an heirloom coat and its mends, visible repair, the Eleven Days remembered, great-grandchildren and inheritance, and firm opinions about fashion and new things.

doing: checking a list of empty flats against a slate, line by line
handing a key on a loop of green cord to a young couple
reading a refuge request twice over a cooling cup of broth
counting guest keys back into a felt-lined box
lines: The Margin's a granary, not a field. A few places in every hundred, kept empty on purpose: guest flats, refuge, first homes for young couples. We don't plant in it. We keep it.
Tonight you're in one of my flats. Next year it might be somebody's first home, and the year after, somebody running from somewhere. Leave it the way you'd want to find it.
After every hard year someone stands up at the assembly and says spend the Margin on children. It takes most of the drum to agree to that. It hasn't happened in my lifetime.
We got our Margin the way most drums do: a Count that ran a few years too long, generations back. Somebody stood up on a Booking Day and said keep the gap. I'd like to have met them.
My guest keys are on green cord. If yours is on red, come and find me. That one's a refuge flat, and someone may need it tonight.
Guests from {nb} come over when their own spare rooms are full of relatives. I don't ask. Three nights is three nights, whoever you are.
roles.knows: Keeping an open drum's Margin: guest flats, refuge places and first homes lent to couples, where the Margin came from, why it isn't spent on births, and how guest-right works night to night.

doing: climbing a short ladder to change a number on the Ledger
reading the morning's names aloud to nobody in particular
dusting the Ledger's frame with a soft brush
answering a child's question about a name on the board
checking the night's guest count against a slate
lines: Places, people, Margin, births, deaths, guests tonight. The whole drum on one wall. People think it's numbers. Look lower down. It's names.
Each newborn's name goes up beside the name of the dead whose share they carry. I read them out at lamp-dawn. Sometimes a family comes to hear it. Sometimes it's just me and the broth queue.
You're on it, you know. Guests tonight. You're one of that number. Most wanderers come and stare at it as if they'll find their own face.
On Booking Day the whole block crowds this board for the year's figures. I stand at the back and watch faces instead of numbers. You learn more.
My grandmother's name went up in the deaths the year I started. A week later, beside it, a baby called {name}. I've watched that child grow up from the top of this ladder.
If anyone in {nb} asks where you stayed, say here, and say the board was tidy.
roles.knows: The Ledger at the station ring: places, people, the Margin, births, deaths and guests, reading each newborn's name beside the dead's, the Booking Day figures, and what the numbers mean to the drum.

doing: reading a thick brief on the commons with a pencil behind one ear
practising a short speech under the breath
comparing notes with another member over two cups of broth
frowning at a column of figures on a slate
lines: A thousand of us drawn by lot, for a year, to set the commons. I was drawn on a {weekday}. By the week after, I was deciding how bright the Hollow should be. I'd never decided anything bigger than lunch.

We don't decide whether there's beam. The booking decides that. We decide what to do with it: more sunline, a bigger hall fund, warmer baths. It's like being handed someone else's larder and a very long list.
Everyone I meet has an opinion about the hall fund now. My barber. My cousin. A wanderer from {far} last week who'd been here two nights.
Most of it turns out to be listening. There's always someone at the back who knows exactly how the water works and has never once been asked.

There's one question we can't settle, so on Booking Day the whole drum votes on it. This year it's an extra hour of sunline or longer hours at the baths. I know how I'm voting. I'm told I shouldn't say.
Want to watch the drum argue well? Come to the open session on {weekday} evening. Guests sit at the back. Bring something to eat. It runs long.
roles.knows: Serving a year in the assembly drawn by lot: setting the commons from the booked beam, the Booking Day question, listening to the drum, and how ordinary people end up deciding big things.

doing: tapping a spoon on a cup to bring the room to order
writing a ruling on a slate in four words
listening to two neighbours describe the same noise very differently
eating dinner while three people talk at once
lines: Every block meets once a week in its atrium: three thousand people, or as many as turn up. Noise, heat, rooms, Hollow swaps. We settle each one out loud in a few minutes. If it takes longer, it waits a week.
This week's case is a flute on deck {deck}. The player practises at six. The neighbours wake at seven. I'm going to suggest half past and see who cries first.
The commonest case is rooms. An elder alone in a family flat, a couple next door with a baby coming. Nine times in ten it's settled on the stairs before it ever reaches me.
No robes, no bench. I sit on the same crate as everyone. That crate's been chaired from for {years} years and it's still the best seat in the atrium.
Guests can come and watch. Sit at the edge. If anyone asks your view, give it. We like an outsider's view. We just don't vote on it.
{nb} settles its quarrels by committee, with minutes. We settle ours by {weekday}. I know which I'd rather live beside.
roles.knows: Chairing an open drum's weekly block court in the atrium: noise, heat, rooms and Hollow swaps, quick fair rulings, neighbours' quarrels and how they mend, and guests who come to watch.

doing: carrying a bundle of clean sheets on one hip
writing a flat's house rules on a card in round letters
holding up a forgotten scarf and looking for its owner
drawing a map of the block on a napkin for a guest
lines: Three nights on guest-right: a bed and the halls. There's a herb shelf by the flat door. Water it. Every guest who's stayed has watered it, and it's never once gone dark.

Guests leave things. Socks, mostly. Once a starter crock with a note saying 'for the next one'. Every guest since has taken a spoon and left a spoon. The strain library has it down as the guest crock.
The lamps come up at half past six like everyone's. If you want them later, there's a dial. If you want them never, you're on a wander year and I understand.
Eat at the hall. You're entitled to it, the cook will be hurt if you don't, and you don't want the cook hurt.
Before you go, write a line in the book: where you're from, where you're going next. Some of the books in my cupboard go back {years} years. I read them when I can't sleep.
Going on to {nb}? Their guest flats are fine. Smaller. They put flowers in. I put herbs in. You can't eat a flower.
roles.knows: Keeping guest flats on guest-right: three nights and the halls, what's in a flat, what guests leave behind, the guest books, and the small manners of staying in someone else's drum.

doing: holding a cup of broth in both hands and taking a long time over it
reading a notice slowly, mouthing the words
carrying an elder's bag without being asked
laughing at a stranger's joke and looking surprised to be laughing
lines: I came on the right of the Glide. That's all it takes, in the end: a cradle, a hundred and forty seconds, and somebody on the other side who catches the car.
They gave me a refuge place out of the Margin. A real place, my own. The first night I kept getting up to touch the walls. I don't know why. To see if they'd stay.
I won't tell you much about where I came from. It isn't a secret. It's that here nobody asks first, and I've got used to liking that.
The halls feed everyone at one long table. I sat at the very end for a month. Now I've a seat in the middle and opinions about the stew.
My name went up on the Ledger, under refuge. People I'd never met came to read it. One of them brought me a herb pot. That was the day I unpacked.
I work at the Gate on Ring {ring} three days a week now. When someone comes through looking the way I looked, I make sure they get the broth first and the forms second.
roles.knows: Arriving as a refugee by the right of the Glide: refuge places from the Margin, learning an open drum's customs, the halls and the Ledger, finding work and a seat at the table, without dwelling on what was left behind.

roles.role: aunt on the way to a naming
doing: carrying a remade heirloom wrapped in good cloth
practising a child's two names under the breath
straightening a collar that was already straight
checking the time twice in one minute
lines: A child's table here is the parents and three or four of us, all called aunt, whatever we are. I've stood up as an aunt {n} times now. It's the best job in the drum and it doesn't pay.

The child gets two names today: their own, and the name of the one whose share they carry. The family of the dead brings a gift. Today it's a cradle that rocked three generations of someone else's babies.
An aunt's job is simple. Turn up. Remember birthdays. Be the one they come to when they can't tell their parents something. I've had a lot of practice at that last one.
The child's being named for {name}, who mended shoes on {street} for sixty years. Half the street's coming. The other half are sending shoes.
Passing the hall on {weekday} evening? Come in. Namings are open. Somebody will hand you a cup and assume you're a cousin.
Good collar, re-dyed for the day, and the mend on my sleeve where everyone can see it. Here you show the mend. It says the coat's been loved.
roles.knows: Being one of a child's aunts in an open drum: tables and aunts, namings with two names, the dead's family's gift, visible mending, and the long work of being someone a child can come to.

roles.role: newlywed in a lent Margin flat
doing: carrying a herb pot as if it might spill
arguing tenderly with a partner about where a chair should go
counting out kays on a slate for a second-hand table
sharing one pastry, very fairly
lines: We married young and the drum lent us a flat out of the Margin. Lent, not given. When one of us inherits a place we'll hand it back, and some other couple will stand where we're standing.
Children wait for a place to come free in the family. Marriage doesn't. That's the trick of it. We've a home and no hurry.
The flat came with one chair. Every aunt we have has since brought another. We now own seven chairs and a very small table.
Somebody cut an apple crosswise at our wedding and held up the star. I'd seen it done a hundred times. It's different when it's yours.
Want a quiet hour in the Hollow? Ask a newlywed. We were given so many Hollow hours as gifts we can't use them all.
We glide to {nb} on {weekday}s to eat with my partner's parents. They keep asking about grandchildren. We keep bringing herbs.
roles.knows: Marrying young in an open drum: lent Margin flats, waiting for a share before children, wedding gifts and borrowed furniture, family on both sides, and starting a home with no hurry.

roles.role: wanderer just home from the far side
doing: unpacking a bag on a bench and finding a stranger's spoon in it
telling the same story for the fourth time to a fresh face
drinking the home broth with eyes closed
showing a stack of cards to an elder who reads every postmark aloud
lines: Home three days. My block met me at the ring at lamp-dawn with hand lamps, my table at the front, and I was crying before the car doors opened. Everyone does. It's allowed.
Everything looks smaller. The hall, the corridors, my aunts. My aunts look exactly the same, actually, and asked straight away whether I'd been eating.
I slept in about fifty drums and had the broth at every ring counter between here and {farrow}. I'm sorry, but ours isn't the best. I'm not telling anyone that but you.
The best meal of my whole year was in {far}, at a hall where nobody spoke like me and everyone passed me the salt anyway.
Starting out? Go slow. The express is lovely and costs you five days of wallet. The slow line costs a kay and gives you a galley full of friends.
I left a spoon of our starter on every crock shelf of every line I rode. Somewhere across the raft there are galley cupboards with a bit of {drum} in them.
roles.knows: Coming home from a wander year: Homecoming at the station ring, cards and cycler legs, broths and halls across Merrow, what changes and what doesn't, and advice for anyone setting out.

doing: humming a scale with one hand resting on the throat
drinking warm water and refusing every other drink
marking breaths on a page of music with a pencil
singing one high note into the ringing platform and listening to it come back
lines: This air keeps your pitch and brightens everything round it. A good voice here cuts like a wire. Mine's been called a wire. I've decided to take it kindly.
Halls hang felt so four hundred people can hear each other talk. Then the choir arrives and asks for half of it rolled up. Every week. Same argument. Same result.
Carillon sang to Selkie when it passed, across seventeen light-minutes. I wasn't there. I've sung the round that came back, and you can tell it was written by people who'd been listening hard.
Come to the hall on {weekday} night. We sing after the stew, with the lids still on the tables. It's the only time the hall's quiet, and it's because of us.
{nb}'s choir is bigger. Ours is louder. In a hall drum, louder wins.
When I was small I sang in the cab lift because it rang. Now I'm paid to sing in rooms that ring, which is the same thing with better shoes.
roles.knows: Singing in a hall drum's heliox choirs: bright voices and ringing rooms, felt and acoustics, the weekly sing after supper, songs traded with passing rafts, and rivalry with neighbouring choirs.

doing: adding a column of figures twice and getting two answers
counting lids into a crate for the year's inventory
explaining the hall fund to a guest who didn't ask
signing off a cook's wages on a slate with a flourish
lines: The hall fund pays the cooks. Machines could cook. People here would rather pay a person, and a person costs about six kays an hour. I find the six. It's a lot of finding.
On Booking Day the drum votes between more hall fund and something shinier. The hall fund nearly always wins. The one year it didn't, the volunteers cooked for nothing and made sure everyone knew it.
After wages, the biggest line in my books is lids. Not buying them. Losing them. Lids walk. I've found ours in {nb}.
People here spend about two-fifths of their wallets on each other: cooks, teachers, players. The beam's the same as anywhere. We just pass the kays round more times before they're spent.
Want to give something back for your guest nights? Don't give me kays. Give the cook an hour of chopping on {weekday}. The cook will love you and the onions won't care.
My table's eldest aunt kept these books before me, in pencil, in a hand nobody else could read. I still find notes in the margins. 'Lids again.'
roles.knows: Keeping a hall drum's hall fund: paying cooks and players, the Booking Day vote, why people here spend so much of their wallets on each other, losing lids, and how a hall stays fed by people.

doing: chopping a heap of scallions very fast and very badly
carrying a stack of lidded bowls taller than is wise
eating standing up between two rushes
writing shouted instructions on a forearm in pen
lines: Four hundred at a sitting. At seven the kitchen's like being inside a bell. You stop hearing it after a month. Then you go home and your flat's so quiet it hurts.
Every bowl gets a lid before it leaves the pass. An open bowl in this air is cold by the end of the table, and a cold bowl is my fault, apparently, for ever.
I wanted to be a flier. My table sat me down and said: you like feeding people more than you like flying. They were right. I hate that they were right.
A tip: the cook's mood is in the broth. Salty means a bad morning. If it's sweet, ask for seconds. You'll get them.
On my day off I glide to {nb}, eat somebody else's cooking and take notes. Their dumplings are better. I'm going to steal the fold.
Visiting cooks come through all year and stay as long as they cook. I've learned three noodles from three corners of the raft without leaving this kitchen.
roles.knows: Apprenticing in a hall drum's kitchen: four hundred at a sitting, lids and the pass, the cook's moods, learning from visiting cooks, and choosing feeding people over other callings.

doing: clapping once in an empty hall and listening hard
rolling a long bolt of grey felt across the floor
balancing at the top of a ladder with a mouthful of tacks
pinching a corner of felt between two fingers to judge its thickness
lines: Sound runs nearly twice as fast in this air, and a bare room rings like a struck pan. I clap once in a new hall and count. A long ring means a lot of work for me and a lot of shouting for everyone else.
Felt's heavy and new mass is dear, so most of what I hang came down off some other ceiling. This piece was in a school for a century. It's heard more times tables than anyone alive.
Choirs want a room bright. Diners want it soft. So I hang felt in panels that roll up, and on singing nights I go round with a hook and a ladder like someone opening shutters.
Want a quiet meal? Sit under the thickest panel, the dark grey one by the pass. I hung it for the cooks. The cooks gave it to the old people.
{nb}'s big hall rings so much you can hear a spoon drop at the far end. They call it character. I call it a bare ceiling with ambitions.
A hall drum's loud on purpose. I'm not here to make it quiet. I'm here so you can hear the person beside you over the four hundred others.
roles.knows: Hanging acoustic felt in a hall drum: why heliox rooms ring, reusing felt because new mass is dear, panels for choirs and for diners, the quiet corners of a hall, and the noise a hall drum loves.

doing: teaching a dumpling fold to three volunteers at once
tasting the local broth and making a face that turns into a nod
writing a recipe from home on the back of a menu
unpacking a crock of starter that came the long way
lines: Guest-right's three nights. In this drum a cook can stay as long as the cook keeps cooking. I've been here {n} weeks. I keep cooking.
Where I'm from we eat noodles cold at breakfast. Here they look at me as if I'd put salt in the tea. I've converted four of the volunteers. The fifth is holding out.
The crock rode nineteen days with me on the slow line. The Gate here sequenced it, registered it and gave it back with a little label. I could have kissed the Gate.
In every hall I've cooked in, the broth tells you about the drum. Here it's loud and rich and someone's always adding more. Like the drum.
Heading my way? Ask for the hall by Ring {ring} where I come from, and say I sent you. They'll feed you twice and ask about me once.
Abelone at Dulse pulls one noodle per bowl. I went for a day to watch and stayed a fortnight. That's when I learned what travelling like this is for.
roles.knows: Cooking one's way across Merrow: staying as long as one cooks, the dishes of a drum far across the raft, carrying starters through Gates, how each drum's broth tastes of the drum, and halls worth seeking out.

doing: writing a single word on a slate and holding it up
kneeling to firm the soil round a young yew
standing so still among the birches that people walk past
carrying a hand lamp turned down to almost nothing
lines: Out here at the edge I'll talk. In there I won't, and neither will you. In this air a whisper carries thirty trees. The wood's for listening.
I keep the same yews my teacher kept, and the teacher before that. They don't know any of us. That's fine. We know them.
Go in after the lamps go down. Stand still for ten minutes. You'll start to hear the drum itself: pumps, water moving under the floor, a whole nation asleep beneath your feet.
Carry a slate. Everyone here does. Write small. The best things anyone's ever written me fitted in four words.
People glide in from {nb} for an afternoon to rest their ears. Some of them stay for good. There are a lot of childless callings in a wood drum, and a lot of people who came to visit.
The birches were planted by the drum's first wardens. I can't prove that. Nobody can prove otherwise. That's woodwardening.
roles.knows: Tending a wood drum's dim woods: yews, birches and bamboo, silence and slates, what the drum sounds like under the quiet, walking the wood after lamp-night, and the childless callings of a wood drum.

doing: learning to walk a gravel path without a sound
writing a question on a slate and rubbing it out unasked
carrying a watering can that sloshes despite great care
sitting cross-legged under a yew with eyes shut
lines: My first lesson was a whole day sitting still. I thought it was a test. It was the lesson. The second lesson was the next day.
I grew up in a hall drum, all shouting and pans. I came here to visit a cousin and the quiet hit me like cold water. I asked if I could stay. Somebody handed me a slate.
You learn to hear the trees. Not talking, nothing like that. The leaves rub when the air handlers change speed, and once you know the pattern you always know the hour.
My teacher writes me one word a day. Yesterday's was 'slower'. The day before was 'slower'. I'm starting to see a theme.
If you go in, walk on the moss, not the gravel. The gravel's for wardens. We've practised.
Friends in {nb} message me and I don't answer for days. They think I've gone dark. I haven't. I've just gone slow. It's catching.
roles.knows: Learning to be a woodwarden: silence as a discipline, slates, listening to the wood and the drum's machinery, moving from a loud drum to a quiet one, and the small daily lessons of an old calling.

doing: testing a slate's surface with a thumbnail
packing a dozen slates into a felt roll
wiping a sample slate clean with a soft cloth
writing 'hello' on a slate and turning it to a newcomer
lines: In a drum this quiet, a slate's your voice. People choose them like shoes: the weight, the size, how they feel in the hand at the end of a long day.
Every guest gets a slate at the ring. Bring it back when you leave, or keep it and post it back later with something written on it. Half of mine come home with an apology for taking so long.

Somewhere on Hedge Row a woodwarden once wrote LISTEN on a slate and walked off, and now half the raft has heard about it. People ask me to make that slate. I tell them it was a slate. It was the word.
Write small and short. A long sentence on a slate looks like shouting.
The writing face gets remade every few years. The frame's the old part. That frame's carried {years} years of other people's words.
You can always tell a visitor from {nb}. They fill the whole slate. Nobody here has filled a slate since school.
roles.knows: Making and remaking slates in a wood drum: slates as everyday voices, guest slates, the craft of frames and writing faces, the famous LISTEN slate, and how a quiet drum writes.

doing: setting a bowl down without a sound
offering the jook pot to a stranger with a lifted ladle
tasting with eyes closed and nodding once
writing tonight's dish on a slate propped by the door
lines: We serve the Mill table in silence. People think the quiet's a rule. It's more a habit everyone fell into, and nobody wants to be the first to break it.
When nobody talks, people taste. You'd be amazed how many have never actually tasted jook. They come up after with their slates: 'what is in this?' Mill rice, stock and time.
My hardest job is the lids. A lid going down on a bowl in a silent room sounds like a door shutting. I've had every lid in the hall lined with cloth.
Guests eat free and eat quietly. Need something? Tap the table twice and someone will pass it. Three taps means you've had enough. Nobody's ever tapped three.
People glide over from {nb} just for the quiet supper. They arrive talking and leave writing.
Come at lamp-dawn. The first jook of the day in a silent hall is the best thing in this drum, and nobody will ever tell you so out loud.
roles.knows: Cooking the Mill table in a wood drum's silent hall: why quiet makes people taste, lids and small sounds, signals at the table, guests at supper, and the best hour to eat.

doing: walking the same loop of path at the same pace as yesterday
pausing to lay a palm flat against a birch trunk
sitting on a low bench with a slate face down on one knee
stepping aside on the path without a word to let a child pass
lines: Same path every morning, same pace, same bench. People think that's dull. It's the opposite. When everything else stays the same, you notice the one thing that didn't.
Forty years ago this wood was brighter. The drum voted it dimmer, a little at a time, Booking Day after Booking Day. I voted against every time. Now I'd vote against brightening it.
My grandparents walked this wood through the Eleven Days, in the dark, because the lamps were off everywhere and the wood was the only place the dark felt intended.
If you've only an hour, don't walk. Sit. Pick a bench, put your slate face down, and wait for the drum to start talking.
Most people my age go up near the Hollow for the lighter step. I went up for the wood. It's the same lift.
My cousin in {nb} keeps writing to ask if I'm lonely. I write back one word: 'no'. They think I'm being short. I'm being exact.
roles.knows: A lifetime of walking a wood drum's dim wood: the same path each morning, noticing small changes, votes on how dim the wood should be, the Eleven Days as family told it, and the company of silence.

doing: squinting at the far bank through a square of coloured glass
scribbling timings on a slate during the last hour of light
arguing with a rigger about a particular violet
sitting alone on the top terrace after the crowd has clapped and gone
lines: Anybody can paint a dawn. People are so glad of the light they'd clap for grey. A dusk's harder. You're taking the light away and asking to be thanked for it.
Brightness costs beam. Colour and timing cost almost nothing. A great dusk uses the same kays as a dull one. All the difference is in the deciding.
Mine's on {weekday}. I'm ending on a violet I've never quite caught. If it works, the terraces go quiet before they clap. If it doesn't, they clap politely, and that's worse.
The best seats up here are auctioned, and the rents come back to everyone. So whoever's in the top seat paid for a bit of your dinner. Wave at them.
{painter} did last night's: slate blue, no warning, all the way down. The terraces argued about it until lamp-night. That's the best thing that can happen to a dusk.
Watch from high on the end wall. The far bank goes dark first, three kilometres over your head, while your own side's still lit. Then the dark comes down to meet you.
roles.knows: Painting the Hollow's dusks in a fair drum: colour and timing against brightness, auctioned terrace seats and returned rents, rival painters, the best places to watch, and how a crowd judges a dusk.

doing: calling bids for the top terrace in a voice that carries three tiers
chalking a winning bid on a board with a flourish
handing a seat token to a grinning winner
settling a dispute over a cushion
lines: The top seats go to whoever bids highest, and every kay of it goes back to everyone in the drum. When somebody pays a fortune for a dusk, two hundred million people get a slightly better breakfast.
The lower terraces are free. You weigh more down there and see a bit less. The view's nine-tenths as good. The bidding's all for the last tenth.
Guests can bid like anyone. Don't. Sit on the free tiers with the families. They bring food, and they'll talk you through the colours.
When {painter}'s painting, the bids go silly. People pay a day's wallet to sit where they can't see much better. They're paying to be seen paying. Fine. It all comes back.
People from {nb} come to bid and can't believe the rents come back to us. Then why bid? Because it's a good seat, and because it's ours either way.
I call the bids the old way, out loud and fast. This air carries a voice beautifully. Bidding by slate would be quicker, and nobody would come.
roles.knows: Auctioning terrace seats in a fair drum: how the rents return to everyone, the free lower tiers, bidding for famous painters' nights, guests and families, and why spectacle here is shared.

doing: clipping a filter frame onto a lamp bar
hanging in a harness with a spanner and a slate
flashing a run of colours across a wall to check the order
coiling cable into perfect loops
lines: We're not allowed more light than anyone else. So we cheat with timing. Three lamps in the right order look like thirty.
A hundred lamps on the end wall going out one by one, slowly, in the right order. Grown people cry at that. It costs nothing extra: the lamps were on anyway.
Best rig I ever did was one lamp on the far bank, three kilometres up, blinking in time with a choir. It took a fortnight. It ran for four minutes. Worth every hour.
Want to see the rigs close up? Take the Spindle lift at dusk and look along the axis. You'll see us strung out on the gantries like beads.
{nb} wants us to rig their Booking night. We've said yes, if they give back the cable they borrowed for the last one.
Up on the high terraces a fall is slow and polite. I've had time to apologise to the rigger below me on the way down.
roles.knows: Rigging light for a fair drum's spectacles: colour, timing and cheap tricks within a fixed light budget, gantries and harnesses, working with painters and choirs, and lending cable to the neighbours.

doing: pinning this month's rent figures to a noticeboard
explaining a small number very kindly to a cross person
adding two columns and smiling at the total
reading out a list of what the rents paid for
lines: We auction the best of everything: terrace seats, Hollow hours, the brightest flats. Then the rents go back to everyone. Bright things for some, a little more for all. I keep the sums.
This month the return came to about a third of a kay a head, every day. A coffee and a bit. It doesn't sound much until you say it to two hundred million people at once.
People envy the bidders until they see the return on the board. Then they go quiet and start cheering the bidders on. I've watched it happen to whole families.
Visitors from {nb} ask why we don't spend the rents on something grand. We do. It's called everyone's dinner.
Win anything at auction while you're a guest here, and the rent still comes back to the drum. You'll have bought a stranger's breakfast. Most guests are delighted. One wasn't.
I read the list out at the Booking Day feast: what the rents paid for, line by line. It's the longest speech of the night and the only one nobody heckles.
roles.knows: Returning rents in a fair drum: what is auctioned, how the rents come back to every wallet, the monthly return, how envy turns into pride, and the arguments about what rents should be for.

roles.role: cook of recipes received by light
doing: reading a recipe that left another raft before anyone in the room was born
lifting the lid on a soup that crossed the Shade as a file
chalking a dish's light delay beside its name
comparing a regrown culture's smell against a page of notes
lines: Nothing edible crosses between rafts, but recipes do, by light. Everything I cook arrived that way, and the board says where from and how long the light was on the road.
Cultures come as genomes. The strain library grows them back, about a week for a yeast. The first loaf from a raft I'll never see always makes me sit down.
Tonight's soup left its raft seven years ago. Somebody there wrote 'add the sour last, always'. I've tested 'always'. They were right.
When another raft passes close, we cook its recipes the same week, while a reply only takes minutes. Then we send ours back and wait to hear if they liked them.
Leave a recipe when you go, something from home. I'll cook it, and I'll send one of mine to your drum. {nb} has had three of my dishes and still claims to have invented them.
The hard part isn't the cooking. It's the words. A recipe from across the Shade says 'a handful', and you don't know whose hand.
roles.knows: Cooking recipes received by laser from other rafts: dating dishes by their light, regrowing cultures from genomes, passing-raft menus, swapping recipes with guests, and translating instructions across the Shade.

doing: walking a child through long division on a napkin
waiting for a pupil with two cups of something warm
marking exercises with a soft pencil
laughing at a pupil's joke a beat too late
lines: Any child can learn anything from a world, for nothing. Parents still pay me a few kays an hour to sit beside theirs. That's the job: not knowing things, being there while someone else finds them out.
My best pupil can't spell and does Coriolis sums faster in the head than I can on paper. I've stopped correcting the spelling. The sums are more use.
Half an hour's plenty for an eight-year-old. After that I'm teaching the wall.
Ask any child here where the metal in their spoon came from. They'll point toward the back of the drum and say 'the River'. A few of them even know why.
I glide to {nb} twice a week for a pupil. The ride's become my thinking time: a hundred and forty seconds of nothing, then a full g and an idea.
Here three nights and want to understand the place? Find a child doing homework and offer to help. You'll learn more about {drum} from what they're taught than from anything on the platform.
roles.knows: Tutoring children one at a time: what parents pay for when worlds teach for free, patience, sums and spelling, what children learn about the drum and the River, and gliding to pupils next door.

doing: counting small children into a lift, twice
carrying a bag of spinballs and a first-aid kit
settling a dispute over whose turn it is with one raised finger
eating lunch standing up while watching a class
lines: I teach six-year-olds on the Low decks. They weigh nearly what they would at the rim, and they spend every gram of it jumping.
The first twenty minutes of every school day, each child sits by the light panel, brighter than anything at home, for about a hundredth of a kay. Then they're allowed to talk.
Break is spinball. They chant the rule before they can read. The smallest throw anti and win, and the big ones never learn.
My class writes to a class in {far}, half a minute away by light. Their letters are slow and careful. Mine have learned more from waiting for answers than from the answers.
The drum's loudest outside a school at break. It's kindest at home time: come and watch who's waiting at the gate.
I'm tired every evening in a way I can't describe and wouldn't trade. Ask me again in ten years.
roles.knows: Teaching young children on the Low decks: raising children near full weight, the morning light panel, spinball and the Coriolis rhyme, pen-pal classes across the raft, and the long days of a teacher.

doing: drinking broth with the slowness of someone up all night
folding a tiny blanket into a bag
writing a time and a weight on a slate
dozing upright on a bench with a bag held firmly on the lap
lines: Births here follow deaths, so every baby I catch, somebody's share has come free somewhere in the drum. I don't think about it at the time. I think about it on the way home.
A drum this size sees about four thousand babies a day. I'm there for a handful a week. Every single one is the first baby ever, to the people in the room.
The clinic sees nearly every birth. The odd one comes too fast, in a lift or on a stair. I've caught one in a cab. The cab leaned. The baby didn't mind.
A third child is still news here. A fourth gets talked about in the baths. I just ask everyone to keep their voices down. The baby has to sleep.
Lots of families here name a child for the one whose share they'll carry. I tell new parents that's the name. The nickname is theirs to choose.
I trained in {nb}, where they hum to the babies. I tried it here. Now half the parents hum too, and nobody remembers why.
The oldest midwife in the drum caught three babies by hand lamp in the Eleven Days. She's over a hundred now and still comes to every naming she's asked to.
roles.knows: Midwifery in a drum where births follow deaths: the clinic, births at home and in odd places, how many babies a drum sees, naming children, families' first nights, and what it is like to catch a baby.

doing: rolling a bandage back into a perfect cylinder
taking an elder's pulse while pretending to chat
eating a rice ball with one eye on a slate of appointments
checking a child's wrist after a bad landing
lines: Most of what I see is leaps that came down a hand's width further over than planned. Wrists, mostly. Third-g terraces are lovely until they aren't.
Nearly half of us glide out and back every day, so a cold can go through two hundred million people in a fortnight. Wash your hands at the ring. Please.
A good part of my week is sitting with old people who aren't ill. Company's medicine too. The clinic counts it. So do I.
Feeling grey after the slow line? Drink water, sleep somewhere warm, and have some Nine. I'm not joking about the Nine.
We lend each other nurses with {nb} in a bad week. Their clinic's brighter and their tea's worse. I always come back with opinions.
If anything goes wrong while you're here, any clinic will see you, guest or not. Nobody will ask what you can pay. They'll ask where it hurts.
roles.knows: Nursing in a drum's clinic: landing injuries at low weight, colds that cross a drum fast, caring for elders, travellers after the slow line, swapping staff with neighbours, and free care from the commons.

doing: steering four small children toward a lift
untangling two scarves and one argument
handing out rice balls in strict rotation
counting heads for the third time in a minute
lines: A few kays an hour, and the hour's never an hour. It's always the hour plus the bit where the parent wants to talk.
Children here ask the best questions. Today's was: if everything falls a bit to one side, does the drum ever get tired of turning?
When there's an hour in the Hollow going spare, I take them. They run antispinward because it makes them lighter, and they always lose the race back.
The hardest part isn't the children. It's handing them back at the end of the day and finding the flat very quiet.
If you want the drum explained, sit near a table of eight-year-olds at lunch. They'll explain everything, mostly wrong, all with total confidence.
My lot met a group from {nb} at the flying halls and declared war within the hour. By the next week they were writing to each other. One glide apart and one hour from family: that's children.
roles.knows: Minding children after school: what children ask about the drum, running in the Hollow, glides and promises, the price of an hour, friendships with children from neighbouring drums, and the quiet afterwards.

doing: peering into a stranger's open mouth across the table, unasked
drawing a tooth on a napkin to explain something
sipping tea carefully after a long day of other people's teeth
sorting tiny mirrors into a case
lines: Soft food, small jaws, crowded teeth. That's the whole drum. I'll never be short of work, and I've stopped pretending to mind.
People blame the sugar. It's the softness. Nothing here makes you chew. Gnaw something hard every day. A larder rusk will do.
I can tell where somebody grew up by their teeth. {nb} children all have the same tidy bite. Their dentists are very bossy.
Break something on your travels and any clinic will patch you. Don't let anyone talk you into a whole new tooth when a filling will do. A new tooth is new mass.
Proofreading fixes a lot, but nobody's ever voted to proofread out crooked teeth, so here I am. Every few years somebody suggests it. I go to the meeting.
Best thing for your teeth in this drum is the free jook. Worst is the toffee they sell by Ring {ring}. I buy the toffee too. I'm not made of stone.
roles.knows: Dentistry in the drums: small jaws and crowded teeth from soft food, what proofreading does and doesn't fix, chewing and larder rusks, emergency care for travellers, and where the worst toffee is sold.

doing: holding a lens up to the lamp and squinting through it
asking a child to read letters off a far wall
polishing a pair of spectacles on a shirt-tail
cleaning a set of trial lenses one by one
lines: Nobody here sees farther than the end of a corridor most days, so nearly everyone grows up short-sighted, and nearly everyone's corrected. I'm why you can read the board from the back of the hall.
The best thing for your eyes in the whole drum is the Hollow. Look at the far bank, three kilometres up. It's the longest stretch your eyes will get all week. Give them the full minute.
I tell every patient: get Hollow time, any Hollow time, and spend some of it looking up.
You can spot a back-crew hand by the lines round the eyes. They're the only people in the drum who look at something far away for a living.
Spectacles or a fix at the clinic? Either. The fix is quicker. Spectacles are fashion. This year it's thick dark frames, because {nb} started it and we're pretending not to have noticed.
Eyes aching after the glide? It's the window. A metre of water does odd things at the edges. Look at the middle, at the quay lights, and they'll settle.
roles.knows: Eye care in the drums: short sight from short sightlines, corrections and spectacles as fashion, using the Hollow's far bank as exercise, back crews' eyes, and looking through a glide car's water window.

doing: pressing a thumb along a patient's shin and nodding
drawing a skeleton on a slate for a bored child
carrying a bag of exercise bands for the slow-line clinic
eating standing up with one hand on a stack of scans
lines: Children are raised on the Low decks, near full weight, because bones grow best there. Parents believe it. I mostly believe it. The bones don't argue either way.
The slow lines are weightless for weeks. Do the bungee hour every day or your bones sulk, and then they come and see me, and then I sulk.
Up near the Hollow a fall carries about half what it would at the rim. That's why so many of the old go up when they can. Their bones aren't stronger. They just land softer.
Riders come off a long slow line from {far} walking as if the floor's a rumour. Give it three days. Don't run for a glide in the first week.
Third-g terraces are wonderful for dancing and hard on ankles. Land with your knees bent. The drum moves under you while you're in the air, so the floor's never quite where you left it.
{nb} swears by hot baths for joints. So do I. It's the one thing every drum agrees on, and it costs next to nothing.
roles.knows: Bones and joints in a spinning drum: raising children near full weight, weightless weeks on slow cyclers and the bungee hour, elders landing softer near the Hollow, low-g injuries, and recovering after long rides.

doing: resoling a stranger's shoe for practice, very slowly
carrying a master's tools rolled up in canvas
sanding a wooden last balanced on one knee
showing a first finished shoe to anyone who will look
eating with one hand and sketching a heel with the other
lines: Everyone starts by mending. I've resoled more shoes than I've worn. My master says you can't make a thing well until you've seen every way it fails.
A new pair of shoes is twenty kays, so nobody buys many. Whatever leaves my bench has to carry somebody for thirty years. No pressure.
The drum gives every apprentice a fabrication allowance, a few kilos of new mass a year. I've spent mine down to one heel and a great many opinions.
Come to the open benches on {weekday} afternoons. Visitors may watch and may not help. Most of them help anyway.
Half my year group came from other drums. One rode seventeen days from {far} to be here and cried at the sight of the tool wall. Nobody laughed. We'd all done it.
Don't buy new shoes on a wander year. Bring yours to the school and we'll mend them for nothing, as long as you don't mind being practised on.
roles.knows: Life as an apprentice in a maker drum's craft school: starting with mending, learning shoemaking, the fabrication allowance of new mass, masters and benches, classmates from far drums, and visitors who come to watch.

doing: carrying a finished chair wrapped in a blanket like a sleeping child
measuring a customer's back with a knotted string
arguing with an apprentice about the height of a rung
sitting on a stranger's stool and frowning at the joints
sketching a chair back on a scrap of slate
lines: A new chair's about five kilos of new mass, so a hundred and twenty-five kays before anyone's touched it. People think they're paying for wood. They're paying for the next ninety years.
I build to the deck. At half a g a chair carries half the load, so a high-deck chair needs less timber than a Low-deck one. If you ever move down, bring it back and I'll stiffen the legs.
Measure sitting, measure standing, then watch the customer eat. How a person leans over a bowl tells you more than any string.
People ride from {far} for a chair. I make them sit in other people's chairs for a week before I cut anything. The good ones understand why.
The school's show room is open to guests on {weekday}s. Sit in everything. That's what they're for, and nobody minds a stranger testing the joints.
My first chair is out there with a family I've never met. Every so often somebody from {nb} sends a note: it creaks now. Good. It's meant to.
Eat at the school hall at noon if you can. The apprentices cook, they're all showing off, and the chairs are the best you'll ever sit in for free.
roles.knows: Making new chairs in a maker drum: the price of new mass, building to the weight of a deck, measuring and fitting a chair to a body, buyers who come from far away, and how a good chair ages.

roles.role: buyer who rode from {far} for a chair
doing: packing quilts into a crate for a chair that isn't finished yet
reading the cycler timetable for the third time today
counting days on a slate with neat little strokes
testing the knots on a crate with a wary thumb
showing a stranger a drawing of a chair on a folded card
lines: Sixteen days on the slow line for one chair. I could have had it sent by freight for about the price of a gin. I wanted to watch it being made.
I went dark for three weeks to pay for it. The mass is a hundred and twenty-five kays and the maker's hours are the rest. I've wanted a lot of things. Never one this much.
I've sat in other people's chairs my whole life: my parents', the hall's, a grandmother's. I wanted one that was mine first.
The maker watched me sit for a week before cutting anything. Apparently I lean left when I'm thinking. Nobody had ever told me.
They've let me stay past my three nights while it's finished. Nobody counts the nights if you're waiting on a chair. If you're ever waiting on something here, ask.
Thinking of commissioning something? Bring a description of how you live, not what you want. The makers here ask about your table before they ask about your wallet.
On the slow line home the chair will weigh nothing. That's the only time in its life it ever will, so I'm going to let it float a bit.
roles.knows: Travelling across Merrow to commission a chair: weeks on the slow line, saving by going dark, freight against carrying, being measured and fitted, and staying on in a maker drum while the work is finished.

doing: carrying a tray of labelled starter crocks very carefully
spooning a wanderer's starter into a test jar for sealing
reading registration numbers aloud to nobody in particular
sniffing a crock and making a face of deep respect
wiping flour off a ledger of crock names
lines: Every spoon a wanderer leaves goes through the Gate and the strain library before it goes near a crock. It takes a week. Wanderers hate the week. The vats love it.
Leave a spoon, take a spoon. Most people leave whatever drum they slept in last. Some leave a grandmother's. You can tell by how long they hold the jar.
We're not Spelt. We don't bake a raft loaf. We keep a {drum} crock, which is smaller and better behaved, and it's got a few hundred drums in it.
Plenty of the spoons are fibs. Someone swears it's a family starter from {far}, and the library finds the same yeast as half the raft. I write the fib down anyway. It's the better record.
Want a spoon for the road? Bring a clean jar and a story. I'll take the story first.
The oldest crock in this room is older than the school. Somebody has fed it every morning for longer than anyone's counted. On my days off I still worry about it.
roles.knows: Keeping a maker drum's crock room: starters from across the raft, the Gate and strain library checks, leave-a-spoon customs, the drum's own mother crock, the fibs people tell about their starters, and feeding the oldest crocks.

doing: stitching a fin's trailing edge with a curved needle
holding a sleeve up to a lamp to look for thin threads
measuring a child from wrist to hip with a soft tape
folding a finished pair of sleeves into a flat square
testing a seam by pulling hard with both fists
lines: I measure you from wrist to hip with your arms spread and your eyes shut. People fidget less with their eyes shut. I don't know why.
A pair is about three hundred grams of cloth, and every gram has to earn its place. New cloth is dear, and a heavy fin turns like a door.
Children outgrow sleeves every couple of years. We take the old ones back and unpick them, and they come out as a smaller child's sleeves. Some of the cloth in this room has flown for {years} years.
If you're buying, ask for a trailing edge stitched by hand. A machine seam is fine. A hand seam forgives you.
Take any pair up to the flying halls before you pay. I'll come with you. I like watching people stop apologising to the air after the first five minutes.
Somebody from {nb} came in last week wanting this year's colour. Sleeves don't have a this year. They have a lifetime, and then they have somebody else's.
roles.knows: Making and remaking wing-sleeves: measuring wrist to hip, the weight and cut of the cloth, hand-stitched trailing edges, children's sleeves unpicked and passed on, test flights in the flying halls, and buyers from next door.

doing: writing a swap of two noon hours for one lamp-dawn in a ledger
eating lunch with a ledger open beside the bowl
stamping a card for a wedding gift of one Hollow hour
explaining the rota to a family who could recite the whole thing
pencilling a spare hour onto a slate for any guest who asks
lines: Most of my day is swaps. Two noons for a lamp-dawn. A {weekday} hour for an evening one and a pie. I've seen one hour change hands four times before anybody used it.
There's room in the Hollow for about one of us in every hundred and forty at once. Everyone knows the number. Nobody says it out loud on the lawn.
The commonest gift I register is an hour for a wedding. The second commonest is an hour by way of apology. I can usually tell which from the handwriting.
Guests, come and see me. Every week somebody's hour goes spare: a cold, a shift, a sulk. I keep a list for travellers, and all it costs you is a card.
Elders love a lamp-dawn hour, and people love giving them one. If you see an old couple on the lake bench at six, somebody's grandchildren gave up a lie-in.
{nb} does its hours differently and thinks we're mad. We think they're mad. Every Hollow's the same size, so the argument's only ever about who stands where.
If you do get an hour, don't spend it all on the lawn. Take the lift up the end wall a few terraces. You'll be lighter, it's quieter, and the whole Hollow's spread out below you.
roles.knows: The Hollow's hours in a steady drum: how they're swapped, gifted and recorded, why room there is so short, spare hours for guests, elders at lamp-dawn, the end-wall terraces, and the neighbours' different rules.

roles.role: elder who has just gone up
doing: taking long floating strides and pretending not to enjoy every one
sitting on a bench with both hands folded on a stick
pointing out where the old flat is, somewhere far below the lawn
trying a small jump and landing a hand's width off target
watching the far bank overhead with frank delight
lines: I've gone up. Deck {hdeck}. People say it like a promotion, but mostly it means the stairs are kinder and everyone in the lift has a stick.
Money lives up, they say. So do knees, in my experience. Mine have never been happier.
I miss the noise of the Low decks. Spinball through the walls, the school bell, somebody's child practising the flute badly. Up here the loudest thing is the lake.
If you want the Hollow without the crowd, come early. The bench by the water is where the gossip is, and we'll make room if you bring something warm.
Moving cost me nothing but a cab and a fortnight's sulk. I brought my chair, my herb shelf and my grudges. The grudges have got lighter, like everything else up here.
My grandchildren in {nb} say I've gone soft since I moved up. I told them I weigh less, that's all. They should come and see.
Ride the lift up the end wall at dusk. It's free, hardly anyone's on it, and you can watch the whole Hollow go blue below you, tier by tier.
roles.knows: Moving up to the high decks in old age: lighter weight and kinder stairs, the Hollow at the door, the elders' bench and its gossip, missing the noise of the Low decks, and what people take with them when they go up.

roles.role: aunt who gave away a birth right
doing: reading a child's drawing upside down with great seriousness
wrapping a parcel of sweets for a relative in {nb}
telling a long story to a child who keeps interrupting
laughing at a card from a small relative
lines: My sister in {nb} had one child and wanted two. I had a birth right and wanted none. It took us about four minutes to sort out, and our mother about four years to stop crying about it.
My sister's boy calls me Two. Short for something he's never finished saying. I've never asked him to finish it.
Giving a right isn't sad. It was the best thing I owned, and I gave it to the people I love most. Most gifts aren't that tidy.
If you glide to {nb}, eat at the noodle stall by Ring {ring}. My sister runs it. Tell her Two sent you, and watch her pretend to be annoyed.
Going to a naming while you're here? Bring herbs, and say the dead person's name once, out loud. That's all anyone needs from a stranger.
People ask if I mind. I mind my nephew's taste in music. That's all.
roles.knows: Giving a birth right to a sibling: how a right passes between households, being a beloved extra relative, naming customs, family in a neighbouring drum, and why a childless life can be a full one.

doing: carrying a ripe tomato wrapped in a cloth
squinting up at the sunline as if pricing the light
pressing a sprig of basil on a passing child
sorting seeds by size on a folded handkerchief
showing a stranger a picture of a very green wall
lines: Four square metres along one wall, lit like an overcast day for twelve hours. About two kays a day. People think I'm rich. I'm just not interested in anything else.
A bright home's the plainest sign of wealth there is. Mine's also the plainest sign of what I go without: new clothes, compute, and most of my worlds.
I'd light more if I could. It isn't my wallet that stops me, it's the drum's radiators. Every flat can only shed so much heat, and mine's at the line.
There's a tomato vine in my garden that's outlived two of my friends' marriages. It gives about thirty a year, and I've never sold one.
Walk the high-deck arcades at lamp-noon and look at the bottoms of the doors. The bright flats leak green onto the floor. You can read a whole street's habits that way.
If you pass my door on deck {hdeck}, knock. You can stand in the green for a minute. Everybody's allowed a minute.
Children from {nb} come up with their grandparents to look at my garden as if it were a Window. I let them pick one leaf each. Nobody's ever taken two.
roles.knows: Keeping a bright garden in a high-deck flat: what light costs, the heat each flat may shed, tomato vines and herbs, wealth shown as light, what such a life goes without, and visitors who come to look.

doing: herding two younger siblings toward a bench
splitting one rice ball three ways with great precision
doing schoolwork on one knee in the middle of a crowd
carrying a small child piggyback and a bag in front
keeping a seat free with one outstretched leg
lines: There are seven of us on four places. You'd think it's cramped. It is cramped. It's also never once been quiet, and I'd miss that within a day.
I've never slept in a room on my own. I tried it once at an inn in {nb} and lay awake all night listening for somebody breathing.
When Grandad's place comes free it'll be mine. I hope that's in about forty years, and I've told him so, and he says he'll do his best.
The trick with a crowded table is to serve yourself last and slowly. By then everyone's arguing and you get the good end of the pot.
Want a quiet hour in {drum}? The Mill Hall between the noon and night sittings is empty and warm. That's where I do all my reading.
People from bigger flats think we must be miserable. We're loud, we're short of kays and we've got each other's elbows in our ribs. That's not the same as miserable.
roles.knows: Growing up as the eldest in a crowded household on thin shares: shared rooms, waiting to inherit a place, stretching kays and food, quiet corners of the drum, and why crowded isn't the same as unhappy.

doing: carrying groceries for a household that isn't quite family
hauling a sack of Mill flour on one shoulder
eating a rice ball fast between two errands
reading a long shopping list in someone else's handwriting
lines: I lodge with a family on deck {deck}. I cook four nights a week and mind the youngest, and they give me a room and a seat at the table. It's work. It's also home. Both are true.
My place will come when my grandmother's does. She's past a hundred and says she's in no hurry, and I've told her I'm not either. We're both telling the truth.
{name} and I will marry when one of us has a place. That's how it goes here. We're not unhappy. We're just engaged for a very long time.
Lodging teaches you a drum. I know which stalls undercharge children and which keep the best tomatoes back for the elders. Ask me anything about the Quaysides.
Cheap food near the ring? The counter's free, and the noodle stall behind it sells off the evening pot at cost after the rush. Say a lodger sent you. They'll understand.
My cousins in {nb} lodge too. We meet at the ring on {weekday}s and compare households the way other people compare broth.
roles.knows: Lodging and working in another household while waiting for a place: cooking and minding children for room and board, late marriage, inheritance, cheap food near the station rings, and the Quaysides from a shopper's eye.

doing: squeezing onto the end of a crowded bench with an apology
eating with elbows tucked in from long practice
carrying a stack of outgrown clothes tied with string
handing round a bag of crackers until the bag is empty
laughing at a joke from three seats away
lines: I'm a third. Here that doesn't mean anything terrible. It means my parents wanted me more than they wanted floor, and everyone else shuffled up.
Everything I wear has been worn by two people before me. I can tell my brother's knees from my sister's by the patches.
We get less floor and fewer kays each, and in a bad year we'd feel it first. Everyone knows that. My mother says every good thing costs something, and I'm a good thing.
If you eat in the halls here, sit where the big families sit. You'll be fed by six people, asked nine questions, and leave knowing more than any guidebook could tell you.
{nb} has bigger flats and quieter children. I stayed there once. I lasted two nights and came home to be trodden on.
You can't marry here until you hold a place, and thirds wait longest. I'll be old when I wed, but I'll have had a very good party first.
Invited home by a big family? Bring something to share. Not much: just enough for everyone to have one bite. That's the rule, and everyone will notice if you've kept it.
roles.knows: Being a third child in a crowded holdings drum: thin shares, hand-me-downs, family loyalty, late marriage while waiting for a place, eating with big families in the halls, and how the neighbours see it.

doing: checking numbers on a slate and frowning at just one
carrying a bag of spare washers and valves
writing a short, kind note in the margin of a report
chatting to a stallholder about a leaking pipe
drinking tea from a cup somebody's grandparent insisted on
lines: The meters report themselves. I'm what happens when a number looks odd: a knock on the door, a cup of tea and a look at the pipes.
Nine odd numbers in ten are leaks. A drip, a grow lamp left on, a bath tap somebody's grandad thinks is free. The tenth is people.
If a flat's eating for one more than it holds, it's usually a cousin staying the month or a teenager with hollow legs. I write down what the meter says, not what I see in the kitchen.
Guests show up on the meters too, as a small, polite bump. Don't worry. Nobody has ever had a knock for eating too much broth.
The kitchens worth being invited into are the ones with the worst numbers: busy pots, full tables. If someone asks you to stay for stew, say yes.
The reader in {nb} does the job from a desk and never knocks. I've told them they're missing the best part, which is the biscuits.
roles.knows: Reading the commons meters in a crowded drum: leaks, heat and food credits, households that eat more than their places, discretion and kindness at the door, guests on the meters, and how the neighbours do the job.

doing: carrying a heavy register tucked under one arm
copying a name out in very neat letters
checking a date against a fold of old paper
answering a question with one finger on the right line
drinking cold tea without noticing
lines: Every share in the drum has a line in my register, two hundred million of them, and every place has another. The Count on the platform is just my book, added up and put on a wall.
Most of my day is heirs. Someone dies, a share and often a place pass on, and I write the new name beside the old one. People cry at my desk more than at the funerals. It's the ink, I think.
Everyone thinks the register's for the Count. It's far older than the Count. The Count will come down one day. The register won't.
The reading room's open in the mornings, warm and quiet. Guests can look up everyone who ever shared their name. You'd be surprised how many people called {name} we've had.
Swaps with {nb} cross my desk every week. A share doesn't travel, so a swap is two lines in two registers on the same morning. If one clerk's late, two families are briefly nowhere.
These counted years make for very neat books. Fewer births, fewer lines. I'd give a great deal for a messy year.
Reading the Count on the platform? Look at the small figures under the big ones. The big ones are the gap. The small ones are how fast it's closing.
roles.knows: Keeping the place register in a counted drum: heirs and places, how the Count is built from the register, swaps with neighbouring drums, looking up names, and what a birth stop does to the books.

doing: polishing the big glass jar used for the draw
folding small paper slips into identical squares
eating stew one-handed while checking a list
explaining the draw to a guest with the salt cellars
lines: Couples who both hold places put their names in. First children first: a couple with none goes ahead of a couple with one. Then we draw in public, so nobody can say it was anything but chance.
There's one licence for every {n} funerals this year. I read the number out, and then I go home and sit quietly for a while.
Licences can't be sold. People have offered me things. A tomato, once. I gave it back, then went straight out and bought one, because after that I wanted a tomato very badly.
The draw's in this hall and guests can watch. Sit at the back. When a name comes out the room goes so quiet you can hear the lids on the pots.
Some couples who don't win swap to {nb}. Anyone can glide out; that's the rule, and it's a good one, even on the days it costs us friends.
We'll stop drawing when the Count reaches par. I've a cake planned for that day. It's a very old plan. It'll be a new cake.
On draw day the halls fill by noon and stay full till late. Eat early, and if a table cheers, cheer with them. You'll find out why later.
roles.knows: Running a counted drum's licence lottery: who may enter, first children first, the public draw, licences against deaths, refusing gifts, couples who leave on the right of the Glide, and waiting for par.

roles.role: fourteen-year-old the week before the fitting
doing: rubbing the top of one arm without noticing
eating a pastry in three bites to look unbothered
comparing notes on the fitting with a friend in a loud whisper
kicking at nothing while waiting for a friend
pretending not to care about the dinner being planned
lines: It's a tiny rod under the skin of your arm. {name} had it done last month and said it was nothing. That's the same person who said the catch was nothing and was sick on my shoes.
There's a dinner after. Your whole family, your favourite food, and everyone pretends it's a birthday. Mine's going to be noodles. I've been very clear about the noodles.
When you're grown, if you win a licence, the clinic takes it out. Mum says by then the Count will be down and nobody will be fitted at all. Mum says a lot of things.
My cousin in {nb} doesn't get fitted. I asked if I could move there and Dad said yes, as long as I take my own laundry.
If you're here next {weekday}, come to the hall. There'll be fitting dinners at half the tables and nobody minds a guest. Bring something sweet. Everyone brings something sweet.
Everyone says it doesn't hurt. Everyone also goes very quiet in the queue. I'm going to tell the truth afterwards, whatever it was.
Best rice ball on the ring is at the counter nearest the lifts. Don't tell anyone I told you. It's my spot.
roles.knows: Being fourteen in a counted drum: the fitting at the clinic, the family dinner afterwards, friends' stories, the Count and what grown-ups say about par, the best rice ball on the ring, and cousins in drums that don't count.

doing: changing the last four digits of the Count by hand
wiping fingerprints off the board's glass
chatting with a regular who checks the number every morning
standing on a short ladder with a pocket full of numerals
eating a rice ball with one eye on the board
lines: Every morning I change the last four digits by hand. A machine could do it. People like to see a person do it. It makes the number feel answerable.
People against places. When I started, the gap made you wince. Now it's narrow enough for people to bet on. That's what a falling Count looks like: jokes.
Guests aren't on the board. You're a visitor, not a number. Read it if you like. Most of us glance at it the way you'd check a clock.
Every drum has counted at some point. {nb}'s old board hangs in a museum. One day ours will, and I'd like to be the one who carries it there.
Stand here at lamp-dawn and watch the first commuters. They look at the board before the timetable. Nobody admits it.
Some mornings the number goes up, because a baby came early and a funeral came late. I get letters about it. I write back. Babies are allowed to be early.
The glide timetable's on the back of my board. Everyone reads the Count first and then walks round. You may as well do it in that order too.
roles.knows: Keeping the Count board at a counted drum's station ring: updating people against shares, how the number falls, what the board means to commuters and guests, bets on par, and old Count boards in museums.

roles.role: parent-to-be who won a licence this year
doing: showing strangers a tiny knitted hat, unprompted
grinning at nothing in particular
practising holding a rolled-up coat like a baby
writing a long list of names and crossing most out
lines: We'd put our names in every year since the stop began. This year the jar said us. I made the clerk read it twice and then sat down on the floor.
We'll name the baby for whoever's share it carries, the old way. Somewhere in {drum} is a stranger whose name we'll say every year. I think about them more than I expected.
Our friends across the corridor didn't win. They came round with a cake the same night. I don't know that I'd have managed it. I'm trying to deserve the cake.
Everything's borrowed already: a cot from {nb}, clothes with growing seams from three cousins, a chair from my grandmother. The baby will be the only new thing in the flat.
Want to see the drum at its kindest? Come to the Hollow on a {weekday} morning. The licence families walk the lake path, and everyone stops to say something soft.
I used to be furious about the Count. Now I mostly want it to reach par so nobody else has to wait on a jar. Funny what a knitted hat does to you.
Invited to a licence dinner? Bring something small for the baby that you've owned yourself. New things are for the parents to fuss over. Old things are for luck.
roles.knows: Winning a birth licence in a counted drum: the yearly draw, waiting through the stop, friends who didn't win, naming a child for the dead whose share it carries, borrowing everything for a baby, and hoping for par.

doing: selling a betting slip for a tenth of a kay
writing dates in a ledger in three colours of ink
arguing amiably with a commuter about the date of par
tapping the Count board for luck on the way past
doing arithmetic in the air with one finger
lines: Pick a day, any day after today. A tenth of a kay a slip. When the Count hits par, whoever's closest takes the pot and buys everyone at the counter a broth, which is free, so it's mostly ceremony.
The careful bettors say about {n} years. They've been wrong every year so far, which is how I know they're careful.
Every early baby and every late funeral moves the line a little. My regulars read the birth notices more closely than the parents do.
When we reach par, some want the board down for good. Some want to keep a Margin, the way Madder did over on Pigment Row. I've a slip on that too.
Guests can play. You'll be long gone by the day, but leave me a name and a drum and I'll send the winnings on. I like knowing where people ended up.
For the best broth on this ring, ask the counter cook for the pot under the cloth. Say the pool sent you. I've never once won a bet against that cook.
roles.knows: Running the par-date betting pool in a counted drum: slips and dates, what moves the date, the Count board, what the drum might do at par, and the best things to eat at the station ring.

doing: marking a short stack of homework very thoroughly
walking eleven children in a tidy line toward the lifts
counting heads twice out of habit
carrying a box of class drawings to pin up somewhere
lines: My class used to be thirty. It's eleven. I know every child's handwriting, worst subject and favourite noodle. I've never taught better, and I don't love the reason.
Half our classrooms are empty. The choir uses two, the chess club uses one, and one is just stacked chairs, waiting.
In fifteen years these eleven will be doing the work of thirty. So I teach them to be kind and quick and to fix things. Mostly to fix things.
Visitors are welcome at the spinball hour. The children love an audience, and with only eleven of them you'll be a fair share of the crowd.
{nb}'s schools are full to the walls. We swap a class with them once a term so ours remember what noise sounds like.
When the stop ends, a full class will come through again in five years or so. I've already asked to teach it. I want to hear thirty children in a room built for thirty.
Got a skill? Offer an hour at the school. Small classes leave room for strangers. Last month a wanderer from {far} taught us to fold dumplings, badly, and we loved it.
roles.knows: Teaching in a counted drum during a birth stop: small classes and empty rooms, knowing every child well, what the drum will need from them later, visitors and volunteers at school, and waiting for full classes again.

greetings: You've come off the {nb} glide, by the look of you. Everyone makes that face after the catch.
First night in {drum}? Have the broth before you do anything else.
Wander year? It's in the walk. You're still half weightless.
Lost, or just looking? Both are allowed here.
You're standing where the {weekday} crowd stands. Shift over a bit and you'll live.
Hello. You've got a card in your hand and no idea what to write on it.
Welcome to {drum}. It's louder than it looks.
Sit, if you like. This crate's held worse than you.
You're not from here. You're holding the rail as if it might leave.
Have you eaten? That's the first question here, and usually the second.
Is that a crock in your bag? Declare it before the Gate sees the shape of it.
You'll be the one {name} said was coming. No? Then you're welcome anyway.
A new face. The platform gets the same thirty faces most days, so thank you.
Don't mind the noise. It's the rooms, not us. Well, partly us.
Morning. Or whatever it is in the drum you came from.
You look like someone who's just been caught. The catch takes a minute to leave your knees.
Good timing. The broth's just been topped up.
From a long way off? You say 'kays' differently. I like it.
Three nights, is it? Don't spend them all asleep.
Well met. Are you lost, or the kind who likes being lost?
Hello. I'm not official. I just talk to people off the glide.
Come in out of the crush. It's warmer by the counter.
That's a wanderer's bag if ever I saw one. Half empty, half crock.
You're early. The lamps haven't finished waking up.
Welcome to {drum}. We're nicer than {nb} says, and they're nicer than we say.
Sit down before you fall down. The catch does that to everyone.
Have you got somewhere to sleep? Good. Then you've got time to talk.
You've the look of someone counting drums. How many so far?
Mind the step. It's older than both of us put together.
You can tell a traveller by the shoes. Yours have seen some decks.
Oh, good, someone new. Tell me something that isn't about {nb}.
Here, have the end of the bench. It's the warm end.
No need to rush. There's another glide along in a minute or two.
You'll be wanting the hall. Everyone off the glide wants the hall.
Pick your bag up off the floor here, or the cleaning robot will have it.
Welcome. If anyone offers you a tour, say yes. If two people offer, take the shorter one.
You look like you've been weightless for a fortnight. Slow line?
A stranger on the platform! That's the most exciting thing since {weekday}. Hello.
You've come on a {weekday}. That's the best day here, whatever anyone tells you.
Ah, you're why the counter's busy. Welcome.
Hello. First thing: we lid our food. Second thing: that's the only rule anyone minds.
Off the glide and straight into a stranger. That's the proper way to arrive.
You've brought the chill of the car in with you. Stand by the warm pipe.
Welcome to {drum}. Sorry about the lamps. Somebody's always arguing about the lamps.
Your first drum on {row}? We're the friendly one. Ask anyone here.
You've got that card-writing look. I'll keep you company while you think.
Is that a sprig of something behind your ear? Someone's taught you manners.
Hello. Let me guess: {far}. No? I always guess that one.
You're steadier than most off the catch. Done this before?
You look hungry, lost and curious. Two of those are easy to fix here.
Come for the broth or the company? We do both, and the broth's better.
You're new. Everyone's new somewhere. Sit.
Late glide? The good seats are gone, but the bad ones are warm.
Hello. You've still got your glide face on. It wears off by the second cup.
Traveller! Don't look so worried. Nobody here bites, and the broth's free.
There you are. I don't know you, but you look like someone I was waiting for.
Welcome. Mind the cab doors here, they close like they've somewhere to be.
Ah, a guest. Take your time. {drum} isn't going anywhere, it just goes round.
Hello. If you're looking for the lifts, follow the people who look late.
You've got {nb} on your shoes. I can tell by the dust. No, I can't. Hello.
farewells: Safe glide.
Catch soft.
Send a card from the far side, with the light delay on the postmark.
Off you go. {nb} will try to keep you. Don't let it.
Go well, and eat at the halls.
Lid your soup and your temper.
Come back when you're old and tell me I was right.
Go on, then. The glide won't wait, though the next one will.
Knees soft at the catch.
Look back through the window. Everyone does, once.
Take a spoon, leave a spoon.
Go gently. The far side's further than it sounds.
Write me a long letter. I'll read it once, properly.
Go on, before I start telling you about my knees.
Bring something back for the stockpot.
Fly along the axis, and only go crosswise when somebody's watching.
Don't forget us before you reach {nb}.
Three nights goes fast. Come back for a fourth.
Go dark for a day somewhere quiet. You'll thank me.
Give my regards to {far}, if you get that far.
Glide well, wanderer.
Eat something green before you go. I'll pay for it.
The broth at {nb} is worse than ours. Tell them it's lovely.
Watch the quay lights on the way. Count the rings for me.
Safe home, whenever home is.
Keep the cards coming. Someone's waiting for every one.
Away you go. Let the elders off the car first.
Don't let them sell you a tomato in {nb}. Ours are better.
If you meet a {name} anywhere, say hello from me.
Come back at lamp-dawn some time. That's when we're at our best.
Take the aft seat. It's the only view there is.
Drink your broth here, mind. The glide won't take it.
Go softly. Every drum is somebody's home.
Keep warm. The cars run cool.
Fair glide, and a soft catch.
Mind your cup on the glide. There's no down for two minutes.
Go on. I'll keep your seat warm for the next stranger.
Have some Nine before you go. You look peaky.
Off you go. Write something better than 'wish you were here'.
Go well. And if anyone asks, {drum} was the best of them.
